document.title: Perturbative quantum corrections and the quantum ring structure of the BPS sector: computing all-loop holomorphic Feynman diagrams in four dimensions by circuit reduction

blocks.source: Perturbative quantum corrections and the quantum ring structure of the BPS sector: computing all-loop holomorphic Feynman diagrams in four dimensions by circuit reduction

Botao Li  
Peking University · GPT Astra · Claude Opus 5.5
Abstract
We compute, at arbitrary loop order, the kernels of the holomorphic Feynman graphs that carry loop corrections to supersymmetry transformations and products.

Building on the holomorphic graph integrals of Wang and the operatope of Budzik, Gaiotto, Kulp, Wu and Yu, we read the operatope current equations as those of an electrical network, with Schwinger times as resistances and holomorphic momenta as injected currents.

Using inductive series, parallel and star–triangle reductions as changes of variables on Schwinger space, we compute every $n$-loop operatope graph of interest here, at arbitrary $n$: its rational Schwinger integrand becomes a polynomial on an explicit product of intervals and simplices, and every Taylor coefficient is a finite factorial sum.
These kernels determine the loop-corrected anomalous supersymmetry transformation of composite operators and the quantum renormalized product that constructs the BPS ring.

As an explicit application, we give every perturbative correction to the supersymmetry transformation in $\mathcal N=4$ Yang–Mills theory, including its action on operators with arbitrary holomorphic derivatives; the one-loop correction is the operator of Budzik and Kulp.

Using the marked higher operations of Gaiotto, Kulp and Wu, we also construct and compute the quantum product of $\mathbf Q$-closed operators and prove that, up to $\mathbf Q$-exact terms, it is associative, graded commutative and unital, supplying the multiplication of the quantum BPS ring.
As a consequence of this ring structure, every multi-graviton operator lifts to a cocycle of the full quantum supercharge, with an explicit and finite all-order completion.
We also construct closed all-order completions of several known fortuitous classes in $\mathcal N=4$ Yang–Mills theory and confirm that they survive at every perturbative order.
1 Introduction
In a unitary superconformal theory, the cohomology of a nilpotent supercharge $Q$ is isomorphic to the corresponding BPS sector.
Each class has a unique harmonic representative, annihilated by $Q$ and its radial adjoint $Q^\dagger=S$.
For $Q=Q^4_-$ in $\mathcal N=4$ Yang–Mills theory, this is the $1/16$-BPS sector [1, Section 2].
The scaling dimensions of these states are fixed by their angular momenta and R-charges, which is the BPS bound.

Quantum corrections to the supercharge (anomalous SUSY transformation) determine which classical classes persist in the interacting BPS spectrum and constrain the microscopic states of dual AdS black holes [17].

In the original physical theory, the full understanding of it requires carefully defining the renormalized product of local operators and their counterterms, which is, in fact, highly technical work. However, a much more effective and elegant approach is studying the holomorphic twist of the theory.

blocks.source: In a fan, the interaction vertices form a path, and each of them is joined to the composite operator we study; every loop correction to the anomalous supersymmetry transformation in a renormalizable theory, such as \(\mathcal N=4\) Yang–Mills theory, is a fan.
We derived the explicit analytic result of the fan kernel at every loop order, computed using the analogy to circuits and iteration.

blocks.source: In a spider, several such paths meet at one vertex, and every vertex is joined to a second vertex. The first vertex is the superpotential \(\bar W\) (which can even be nonrenormalizable, and when it is cubic, the spider kernel comes to the fan); the second is the composite operator we want to study. This exhausts all kinds of anomalous SUSY transformations in 4d N=1 SUSY gauge theories, renormalizable or not.

blocks.source: 2 Summary of results
2.1 Graph kernels as circuits

The loop corrections to the supersymmetry transformation of a holomorphic local operator $\mathcal O$ are higher brackets [15] with the interaction $\mathcal I$ [6, Equation (3.33)], [16], given by the holomorphic graph integrals of [7; 8] (Section [3](#sec-setup)):

\mathbf Q=\sum_{n\ge0}\hbar^nQ_n,\qquad
Q_n\mathcal O=\frac1{(n+1)!}\{\mathcal I^{\otimes(n+1)},\mathcal O\}_0 .\tag{2.1}
The bracket is a sum over connected graphs $\Gamma$ with $n+1$ interaction vertices and one insertion.
Each graph contributes its Wick contractions times the computational kernel operatope \(\mathcal I_\Gamma^{\mathrm{raw\ cut}}(\lambda;z)\) of (B.11).
With the edge currents $y_{e,+\dot a}$ of (B.15), the initial and final vertices $e(0)$, $e(1)$ of each oriented edge $e$, and a spanning tree $T$, the kernel is (B.21)
where $\Delta_\Gamma$ consists of the currents that obey $\sum_{e\in C}\pm t_ey_{e,+\dot a}=0$ around every loop $C$ for one common set of positive Schwinger times $t_e$ (3.8).
These are the equations of an electrical network [21; 22], read from those of the operatope [8, Equations (2.26), (2.31), (2.33)] (Table 1).

Let the interaction be (3.6), $\mathcal I=-\frac g2C^A{}_{BC}\mathsf b_A\mathsf c^B\mathsf c^C-ig\mathsf c^A(t_A)^j{}_i\gamma_j\beta^i+\bar W(\gamma,\mathsf w)$, with $\bar W$ of any degree.

Proposition 2.2 (Further constraints on the graphs).
In the setting of Proposition 2.1:

(i) Every nonzero graph of $Q_n$, and of the quantum product at order $\hbar^n$, has $n+2$ vertices and $2n+1$ edges, no self-loops and no parallel edges, and $|\Gamma_1[S]|\le2|S|-3$ for every vertex set $S$ with $|S|\ge2$.

(ii) A nonzero connected graph of $Q_n$, $n\ge1$, contains at most one $\bar W$ vertex, and each of its terms lowers the number of $\mathsf b,\beta$ factors by $n$ plus the number of $\bar W$ vertices.
(iii) In a nonzero graph of the quantum product, every interaction vertex has degree at least two, and loop diagrams contain no quadratic term of $\bar W$.
A tree whose $\bar W$ vertex has $\deg_\Gamma\bar W$ contracted fields contains $\deg_\Gamma\bar W-2$ cubic vertices of degree two and keeps $\deg\bar W-2$ uncontracted fields.

(iv) For cubic interactions, the number of spokes at each vertex of a tree is fixed by its tree degree and by whether it is the vertex of degree two [(6.5)](#eq-product-local-spokes); conversely, the edge $AB$, a forest, and spokes obeying [(6.5)](#eq-product-local-spokes), with one vertex of degree two in each tree, form a graph satisfying (i).

blocks.source: Theorem 2.4 (Exact jets in polynomial time).
Let the interaction be (3.6), with the superpotential $\bar W$ a polynomial or, coefficientwise, a formal power series of $\bar\phi$ and $\bar W_{\dot a}$.

For a graph of $Q_n$, a jet coefficient of order $m$ is the coefficient, in (4.15) or (6.15), of one monomial in the source–source and source–displacement pairings, treated as independent symbols, of total degree $m$ in the displacements (holomorphic derivatives).

blocks.source: (i) For every $n\ge1$ and every graph of $Q_n$, every jet coefficient is a rational number, a finite sum of terms, each a product of $O(n+m)$ factorials and ratios of factorials of integers at most $n+m+2$.

(ii) For an $n$-loop fan put $N_\Gamma=\tfrac12n(n+1)+n+2$ and $T_\Gamma=1$; for a spider with arms $\ell_1,\ldots,\ell_a$ put $N_\Gamma=\sum_i\tfrac12\ell_i(\ell_i+1)+(n+1)(a+1)$ and $T_\Gamma=\prod_{i=1}^a\binom{\ell_i+a-1}{a-1}$.
All jet coefficients of order at most $m$ are obtained exactly with $O\bigl((n+m)\,T_\Gamma\binom{m+N_\Gamma}{N_\Gamma}\bigr)$ arithmetic operations.
This is polynomial in $m$ at fixed $n$, and polynomial in $n$ at fixed $m$ and $a$.

For $\bar W$ of fixed degree, and in every theory with cubic interactions, the graphs of $Q_n$ are the fan and at most $\sum_{a<\deg\bar W}\binom{n-1}{a-1}$ spiders, so at fixed $m$ all jets of order at most $m$ of all kernels of $Q_n$ are computed in time polynomial in $n$.

(iii) For the $n$-loop fan with sources at the endpoints of the path, each jet coefficient of order $m$ costs $O(n(m+1)^2)$ operations, linear in $n$, so all coefficients of order at most $m$ are computed with $O\bigl(n(m+1)^2\binom{m+2n+2}{2n+2}\bigr)$ operations, polynomial in $n$, $m$ and their number.

(iv) For cubic interactions and each graph of the quantum product, the Taylor coefficients of order at most $m$ in the displacements (holomorphic derivatives) are polynomials in the sources with rational coefficients, obtained in time polynomial in $m$.
The proof is in Appendix [B.15](#sec-B-jets); part (iii) rests on a nested Beta recursion, Lemma [B.7](#b-01406).<sup>8</sup>

blocks.source: Lemma 2.6 (Derivative grading).
A monomial has two holomorphic derivative totals, its numbers of $\partial_{+\dot+}$ and $\partial_{+\dot-}$ derivatives.
A class can be $d_r$-exact, for the successive differential $d_r$ of Section 8.3, only if both derivative totals of its leading representative are at least $r$.
In particular, a class whose leading representative has no holomorphic derivatives is $d_r$-exact for no $r\ge1$.

blocks.source: Uses of the quantum product.
The quantum product gives closed completions, which the naive classical (Wick) product does not.
(a) Multi-gravitons remain quantum cocycles.

In $\mathcal N=4$ Yang–Mills theory the single gravitons, the components $G$ of $\operatorname{Tr}(dC)^p$ [1, Section 4], satisfy $Q_nG=0$ for every $n$ (8.7): the fan kernel contains $\prod_{j=1}^n\prod_{I=1}^3(\theta_I^{(j)}-\theta_I^{(j+1)})$, which needs $3n$ odd derivatives, while the $n+1$ contracted factors of $dC$ supply at most $n+1$, so every single graviton is a quantum cocycle; at one loop this is [16, Section 3.4.1].
The quantum product guarantees that multi-gravitons are quantum cocycles as well: every iterated quantum product $\mathcal O$ of single gravitons $G_1,\ldots,G_m$, with any bracketing, satisfies

\mathbf Q\mathcal O=0,\qquad
\left.\mathcal O\right|_{\hbar=0}=G_1\cdots G_m,\tag{2.16}

and each fixed component has finitely many corrections: with $\deg_\theta$ equal to $0,1,2,3$ on $\mathsf c,\gamma,\beta,\mathsf b$ [(8.9)](#eq-2-62), the coefficient of $\hbar^n$ vanishes once $3n>\deg_\theta(G_1\cdots G_m)$ (Theorem [8.1](#b-00630)).
(b) Dressed classes are completed by one more product.

Once a class $\mathcal O_0$ has a closed completion $\mathcal O[\mathcal O_0]$, every graviton-dressed class $G\mathcal O_0$ is completed by $G\star\mathcal O[\mathcal O_0]$, with no new obstruction calculation: once $\mathcal O_0$ has a closed completion, the dressed class needs no closure test of its own.
(c) Higher differentials vanish on completed classes.
A class with a closed completion is annihilated by every $d_r$ (8.39).12 In $\mathcal N=4$ Yang–Mills theory with gauge group of finite rank, in each charge sector and cohomological degree $k$,
\sum_{r\ge1}\operatorname{rank}d_r^k\le\#\{\text{fortuitous classes of degree }k\},\tag{2.17}
and fortuitous classes are sparse among the classical classes known so far [20; 18].

12 We remind the reader that such a class is a quantum cocycle, lifted exactly when it becomes a quantum coboundary: it survives unless it is $d_r$-exact for some $r\ge0$, and a leading representative without holomorphic derivatives is $d_r$-exact for no $r\ge1$ (Lemma 2.6).
A closed multi-graviton can still be the exact member of a lifted pair, as in the one-loop $SO(7)$ example of [17, Section 3], and no differential maps one graviton class to another.
(d) The ring is explicit.
Theorem 2.8 gives the multiplication on $H(\mathbf Q)$, the perturbative quantum BPS ring of $\mathcal N=4$ Yang–Mills theory, and (2.14) computes it graph by graph.
(e) Closure tests reduce to generators.

Since every $d_r$ is a derivation of the product on $E_r$ (8.37), it is fixed by its values on algebra generators of $E_r$; on products of single gravitons every $d_r$ vanishes by (a) and (c), and on a product of classes on $E_r$ it is fixed by its values on the factors.
For the classes known so far, mostly multi-gravitons, this reduction is immediate; it applies unchanged once fortuitous generators are included.
2.6 Loop obstructions and lifting beyond one loop
From the second page on, $d_r$ is not the class of $Q_r$: for a class surviving one loop, with $Q_0\mathcal O_1=-Q_1\mathcal O_0$,

Q_0Q_2\mathcal O_0=Q_1Q_0\mathcal O_1,\qquad
d_2[\mathcal O_0]_2=[Q_2\mathcal O_0+Q_1\mathcal O_1]_2,\tag{2.18}

and $d_2[\mathcal O_0]_2=0$ if and only if $Q_2\mathcal O_0+Q_1\mathcal O_1\in\operatorname{im}Q_0+Q_1\ker Q_0$, with $\ker Q_0$ in the first-correction sector (8.45).13 A cocycle survives at every perturbative order if it admits a closed completion and is $d_r$-exact for no $r\ge0$, where $d_0=Q_0$ (Section 8.3).
Our algorithm for these tests is given in Appendix E.
<sup>13</sup> Algorithmically, a rational linear functional that vanishes on $\operatorname{im}Q_0+Q_1\ker Q_0$ but not on $Q_2\mathcal O_0+Q_1\mathcal O_1$ certifies $d_2[\mathcal O_0]_2\ne0$.
Two-loop lifting.
In massive supersymmetric electrodynamics with
\mathcal I=ig\mathsf c(\gamma_+\beta^+-\gamma_-\beta^-)+\frac m2\gamma_s^2+y\gamma_s\gamma_+\gamma_-,\qquad gmy\ne0,\tag{2.19}
the cocycle

\mathcal O_0=ig\Big[\beta^+\beta^-\mathsf b^2
+\frac ym(\gamma_-\beta^--\gamma_+\beta^+)\beta^s\mathsf b^2
+\frac{y^2}{3m\,ig}\gamma_+\gamma_-\mathsf b^3\Big]
\partial_{+\dot a}\mathsf c\tag{2.20}
has a one-loop completion, is not $d_1$-exact by its derivative totals $(1,0)$ (Lemma [2.6](#b-00094)), and is lifted at two loops:

d_2[\mathcal O_0]_2
=-\frac{2(ig)^2y^4}{m^2(64\pi^2)^2}\Big[
\partial_{+\dot a}(\gamma_+\gamma_-)
\,\partial_{+\dot b}\partial_{+\dot c}(\gamma_+\gamma_-)
\,\partial_+{}^{\dot b}\partial_+{}^{\dot c}(\gamma_+\gamma_-)
\Big]_2\ne0.\tag{2.21}

To our knowledge this is the first example of two-loop lifting (Section [9.1](#sec-SQEDlift)); it answers, for this theory, the question left open in [16, Section 1], although, somewhat disappointingly, none of the fortuitous classes tested here is lifted beyond one loop: each survives at every perturbative order.
Protected classes in $\mathcal N=4$ Yang–Mills theory.
Every $\mathcal N=4$ class tested here survives at every perturbative order (Section [9](#sec-applications)).

• The $18$ multi-graviton classes of the four-letter $SU(2)$ sector of Section [9.2](#sec-finite-sectors) have closed completions ending at order $\hbar$, and the $9$ classes of the five-letter $SU(3)$ sector of flavour weight $(3,3,2)$ closed completions ending at order $\hbar^2$; for the class [(9.21)](#eq-su3-example-source), $Q_2\mathcal O_0=0$ but $Q_1\mathcal O_1=-Q_0\mathcal O_2\ne0$.

• The threshold fortuitous class of $SU(2)$ [18, Section 3.1] has the closed completion $\sum_{r=0}^4\hbar^r\mathcal O_r$ (9.26): each order removes one letter and three units of $\deg_\theta$ and adds two holomorphic derivatives, from $7$ letters at $r=0$ to $3$ letters with $8$ derivatives at $r=4$, and $\mathcal O_4$ has the coefficients $-42731/432$, $23323/216$ and $90043/432$ times $(ig)^3/(32\pi^2)^4$ (9.28).
Although $Q_2\mathcal O_0\ne0$, $d_2[\mathcal O_0]_2=0$.
The leading term has no holomorphic derivatives, so the class is $d_r$-exact for no $r\ge1$ (Lemma 2.6) and survives at every perturbative order, as argued from charge counting in [24, Section 3].

• The three graviton-hair classes of the threshold class [18, Section 3.2] are completed by $(w_2)^I\star\mathcal O[\mathcal O_0]$, with the two-letter single graviton $(w_2)^I$ of [(9.15)](#eq-w2), by its descendant $\varepsilon_{IJK}Q_+^IQ_+^J\bigl((w_2)^K\star\mathcal O[\mathcal O_0]\bigr)$, and by the quantum product of the graviton factor of [(9.35)](#eq-hair-derivative) with $\mathcal O[\mathcal O_0]$; with an explicit check that the last is not $d_1$-exact, all three survive at every order.
Quartic deformation.

In the $SU(2)$ theory with $\bar W=-\frac1{2M}\operatorname{Tr}[\gamma^1,\gamma^2]^2$, $M\ne0$, obtained from $\mathcal N=4$ Yang–Mills theory by a mass for one adjoint chiral multiplet, the supercharge contains spider kernels.

The square $w^2$ of the graviton $w$ (9.40) of [19] has a closed completion ending at order $\hbar^3$, with $Q_2\mathcal O_1=0$ and $Q_3\mathcal O_0$, $Q_1\mathcal O_2$, $Q_0\mathcal O_3$ proportional to one operator with coefficients $-16$, $-42$, $58$; the non-graviton class $\mathcal O_{16}$ of [19] has a closed completion ending at order $\hbar^4$.
Both survive at every perturbative order (Section 9.4).

blocks.source: Quadratic terms of $\bar W$.
A quadratic term of $\bar W$ is a node with two terminals, both wired by the previous step, so it injects no current.
It is the only \(\bar W\) node of its tree, whose \(3(|T_j|-1)+2=3|T_j|-1\) terminals are then all wired by the \(|T_j|-1\) internal resistors and the \(|T_j|+1\) spokes.
The tree carries no source, and the first step gives zero.

A source at a vertex is supplied by its uncontracted fields. For cubic vertices the count is one; if $T_j$ contains a superpotential monomial,

$$ \begin{aligned} \#(\text{uncontracted fields in }T_j) &=3(|T_j|-1)+\deg\bar W-2(|T_j|-1)-(|T_j|+1)\\ &=\deg\bar W-2,\\ \#\{v\in T_j:\lambda_v\ne0\} &\le\#(\text{uncontracted fields in }T_j)=\deg\bar W-2. \end{aligned} $$

Thus the bound is one for cubic interactions, and is not uniformly one for arbitrary $\bar W$.

blocks.source: A spider consists of paths meeting only at a vertex $A$, together with a second vertex $B$ joined to every vertex of these paths, including $A$.
In the supercharge \(Q_n\) graphs, \(A\) carries \(\bar W\) and \(B=\mathcal O\).
The \(i\)th arm contains \(\ell_i\) cubic vertices, labelled \(v_{i,1},\ldots,v_{i,\ell_i}\) from its outer end towards \(A\); its length is \(\ell_i\) and the loop number is \(n=\sum_i\ell_i\).

blocks.source: Each merge lowers the loop number by one.
When every arm is reduced, its branch and the original edge $AB$ merge into one resistor, whose Schwinger time is fixed to one.
Appendix B.10 derives the resulting chart of edge Schwinger times (B.57), with coordinates

0<r_{i,j}<1\quad(j<2\ell_i),\qquad
r_{i,2\ell_i}>0,\qquad\sum_i r_{i,2\ell_i}<1.\tag{6.9}
Here \(r_{i,2j-1}\) is the fraction of the source at \(v_{i,j}\), after the earlier eliminations, that the series step passes to \(v_{i,j+1}\), the rest going to \(B\);
for \(j<\ell_i\), \(r_{i,2j}\) is the fraction of the merged spoke current at \(v_{i,j+1}\) carried by the new branch;
and \(r_{i,2\ell_i}\) is the fraction of the final current carried by the branch of arm \(i\), the original edge \(AB\) carrying \(1-\sum_ir_{i,2\ell_i}\).

The final resistor carries the reduced current $y^{\mathrm{red}}_{AB}$, which by conservation at $A$ is the source collected at $A$: $\lambda_A$ and, from each arm, the fraction of its source passed along the whole arm,
Reversing the reductions splits \(y^{\mathrm{red}}_{AB}\) back into the original currents (B.65)–(B.66).

blocks.source: Proof.

(i) By Proposition B.5(ii), every tree is an arm $v_{i,1}-\cdots-v_{i,\ell_i}$ whose nodes are all wired to one insertion, with the source at $v_{i,1}$ and a resistor from $v_{i,\ell_i}$ to each insertion.

On an arm wired to $B$, the two resistors of $v_{i,1}$ end at $v_{i,2}$ and $B$, which are joined, so Theorem B.2 removes $v_{i,1}$ and passes the fraction $r_{i,1}$ of its source to $v_{i,2}$, which then has two resistors in turn.
The source that reaches the last node of the arm is $\prod_kr_{i,2k-1}\lambda_{v_{i,1}}$, and the last move passes it to $A$ across the marked resistor, as for the spider (6.10).

blocks.source: 8 Multi-graviton completions and obstruction equations
Quantum multiplication constructs perturbatively closed multi-graviton operators in $\mathcal N=4$ Yang–Mills theory.

We prove their closure at arbitrary loop order (Theorem 8.1) and, for illustration, evaluate an explicit product (Section 8.2).28 We then use the operators $Q_n$ to test which classical classes are lifted: the successive transfers of Section 8.3 compute the perturbative obstructions of classical representatives and decide which of their closed completions are quantum coboundaries.

blocks.source: The most direct one-loop example is the lifting of a black-hole class by the Konishi correction: in $SO(7)$ theory, the one-loop supercharge pairs a multi-graviton with a fortuitous class [17, Section 3], and by the theorem the multi-graviton is the exact member of the pair.

Since every graviton class has a closed completion, no differential maps one graviton class to another (Section 8.3); a lift pairs a fortuitous class with a graviton class or with another fortuitous class.

Quantum closedness of a classical representative $\mathcal O_0$ means that corrections $\mathcal O_1,\mathcal O_2,\ldots$ exist with $\mathbf Q(\mathcal O_0+\hbar\mathcal O_1+\hbar^2\mathcal O_2+\cdots)=0$; $\mathcal O_0$ itself is in general not annihilated by $\mathbf Q$ (Section 8.3).
Nonperturbative corrections can also modify the cohomology.
8.1 Perturbative closure of multi-gravitons
In matrix notation,

\begin{gathered}
C=C^At_A,\qquad \operatorname{Tr}(t_At_B)=\delta_{AB},\\
\gamma^I=\delta^{AB}(\gamma^I)_Bt_A,\qquad
\beta_I=(\beta_I)^At_A,\qquad
\mathsf b=\delta^{AB}\mathsf b_Bt_A,\qquad
\mathsf c=\mathsf c^At_A.
\end{gathered}\tag{8.1}
The single-graviton representatives of Chang and Yin [1, Section 4] are components of $\operatorname{Tr}(dC)^p$, where

dC=dx^{+\dot a}\frac{\partial C}{\partial x^{+\dot a}}
+d\theta_I\frac{\partial_LC}{\partial\theta_I}.\tag{8.2}
Theorem 8.1.
Let $G_1,\ldots,G_m$ be single-graviton representatives.
Every iterated quantum product $\mathcal O$ of these operators, with any fixed bracketing, satisfies

\mathbf Q\mathcal O=0,\qquad
\left.\mathcal O\right|_{\hbar=0}=G_1\cdots G_m.\tag{8.3}
For each fixed component, its perturbative completion has finitely many terms.
Proof.
The classical differential acts on a single graviton by
Q_0(dC)=[C,dC],\qquad Q_0\operatorname{Tr}(dC)^p=\operatorname{Tr}[C,(dC)^p]=0.\tag{8.4}
At order $n\ge1$, the odd part of the fan kernel contains

\prod_{j=1}^{n}\prod_{I=1}^{3}
\bigl(\theta_I^{(j)}-\theta_I^{(j+1)}\bigr).\tag{8.5}
A nonzero coincident value requires at least $3n$ odd derivatives.
Each of the $n+1$ contracted factors of $dC$ supplies at most one, leaving degree $3n-(n+1)=2n-1>0$ in the relative odd coordinates.
The kernel therefore vanishes when those coordinates coincide.
Taking a superfield component differentiates in the common odd coordinate; this derivative annihilates every relative difference,
\Big(\sum_{j=1}^{n+1}\frac{\partial_L}{\partial\theta_I^{(j)}}\Big)(\theta_J^{(k)}-\theta_J^{(k+1)})=0,\tag{8.6}
so for every single-graviton component $G$,
Q_0G=0,\qquad Q_nG=0\quad(n\geq1).\tag{8.7}
Thus each single graviton is closed under the full $\mathbf Q$.
At one loop, this closure of the single-trace gravitons and the factor (8.5) are in [16, Section 3.4.1 and Equation (3.70)].

The leading term of each binary product is ordinary multiplication, giving the stated classical limit [1, Section 5].
For termination, $\deg_\theta$ counts the degree occupied by a component in $C$:
\deg_\theta\mathsf c=0,\quad\deg_\theta\gamma=1,\quad\deg_\theta\beta=2,\quad\deg_\theta\mathsf b=3,\qquad\deg_\theta(\partial_{+\dot a}X)=\deg_\theta X,\tag{8.9}
An order-$n$ product graph has $n$ cubic vertices and $2n$ physical edges.
Each vertex contributes degree three, and each physical edge pairs components whose degrees sum to three.
Consequently,
\deg_\theta\mathcal O_n=\deg_\theta\mathcal O_0+{3n}-{6n}=\deg_\theta\mathcal O_0-3n,\qquad\mathcal O_n=0\quad\text{if }3n>\deg_\theta\mathcal O_0.\tag{8.10}
The same degree loss adds under iterated products.
Thus the coefficient of $\hbar^n$ vanishes whenever $3n>\deg_\theta\mathcal O_0$.
For $Q_n$, the $n+1$ cubic vertices and $2n+1$ edges similarly give

\deg_\theta(Q_nX)
=\deg_\theta X+3(n+1)-3(2n+1)=\deg_\theta X-3n\tag{8.11}
whenever the result is nonzero.

Each of the $n$ resistors in the chain of a fan carries the odd factor of [(8.5)](#eq-graviton-odd-factor), and the $n+1$ graviton letters wired to the operator by the spokes supply fewer odd derivatives than the chain consumes.
The graviton part of the cohomology.
At finite rank the classical cohomology consists of a graviton part, spanned by multi-graviton classes, and the remaining fortuitous classes [20].

Theorem 8.1 supplies every class of the graviton part with an explicit closed completion: write its classical representative as a polynomial in single-graviton representatives and replace each product by a quantum product.
By Theorem 5.2, the resulting class is independent of the bracketing and of the order of the factors.

blocks.source: Every successive differential vanishes on it (Section 8.3), so the completed class is a quantum cocycle, lifted exactly when it becomes a quantum coboundary, as in the example of [17, Section 3].

The same construction applies to a graviton-dressed fortuitous class $G\,\mathcal O_0$: once the fortuitous core $\mathcal O_0$ has a closed completion $\mathcal O[\mathcal O_0]$, the product $G\star\mathcal O[\mathcal O_0]$ is closed.
Section 9.3 applies this to the threshold class.

8.3 Homotopy transfer and successive obstructions
The quantum differential acts on a completed representative $\mathcal O=\sum_{r\ge0}\hbar^r\mathcal O_r$ through
Successive contractions.
Let $E_0$ be the complex of holomorphic local operators and set $d_0=Q_0$.
The pages are iterated cohomologies,

\begin{gathered}
E_1=H(Q_0),\qquad
E_2=H\bigl(H(Q_0),d_1\bigr),\qquad
E_3=H\bigl(H(H(Q_0),d_1),d_2\bigr),\\
\ldots,\qquad
E_{r+1}=H(E_r,d_r),
\end{gathered}\tag{8.22}
each the quotient of the kernel of $d_r$ by its image.
The first differential is $d_1[\mathcal O_0]_1=[Q_1\mathcal O_0]_1$, and $Q_1^2=-(Q_0Q_2+Q_2Q_0)$ gives $d_1^2=0$.
From the second page on, $d_r$ is not the class of $Q_r$.
For a class of $E_2$, with $Q_0\mathcal O_0=0$ and $Q_0\mathcal O_1=-Q_1\mathcal O_0$,
Q_0Q_2\mathcal O_0=-Q_1^2\mathcal O_0=Q_1Q_0\mathcal O_1,\tag{8.23}
which need not vanish, while $Q_2\mathcal O_0+Q_1\mathcal O_1$ is closed (8.30).
Each $d_r$ is transferred from $\mathbf Q$ through the contractions of the earlier pages, and $d_r^2=0$ on $E_r$ (8.27).
Choose an inclusion $i_r:E_{r+1}\to E_r$ of cohomology representatives, a projection $\pi_r:E_r\to E_{r+1}$, and a homotopy $h_r:E_r\to E_r$ of degree $-1$, satisfying
These maps separate representatives from exact pairs.
Write $\mathbf Q^{(0)}=\mathbf Q$.
The differential $\mathbf Q^{(r)}$ on $E_r[[\hbar]]$ has constant term $d_r$.
Its transferred differential and corrected maps are

\begin{aligned}
i_r(\hbar)
&=\bigl[1+h_r(\mathbf Q^{(r)}-d_r)\bigr]^{-1}i_r,\\
\pi_r(\hbar)
&=\pi_r\bigl[1+(\mathbf Q^{(r)}-d_r)h_r\bigr]^{-1},\\
h_r(\hbar)
&=\bigl[1+h_r(\mathbf Q^{(r)}-d_r)\bigr]^{-1}h_r,\\
\mathbf Q^{(r+1)}
&=\frac1\hbar\pi_r(\mathbf Q^{(r)}-d_r)i_r(\hbar),
&d_{r+1}&=\left.\mathbf Q^{(r+1)}\right|_{\hbar=0}.
\end{aligned}\tag{8.25}
The inverses are formal geometric series; their order-$\hbar^k$ coefficients contain finitely many terms.
For example, the inclusion satisfies
The second line follows from $d_rh_r=1-i_r\pi_r-h_rd_r$ and $(\mathbf Q^{(r)})^2=d_r^2=0$.
Multiplying by the inverse in (8.25), and applying the corresponding calculation to the projection and homotopy, gives
Thus each new obstruction is itself a differential.
The first obstruction maps.
Writing $[\hbar^k]$ for the coefficient of $\hbar^k$, the first transfer has coefficients

\begin{aligned}
[\hbar^0]\mathbf Q^{(1)}&=\pi_0Q_1i_0,\\
[\hbar]\mathbf Q^{(1)}&=\pi_0(Q_2-Q_1h_0Q_1)i_0,\\
[\hbar^2]\mathbf Q^{(1)}&=\pi_0\bigl(
Q_3-Q_2h_0Q_1-Q_1h_0Q_2
+Q_1h_0Q_1h_0Q_1\bigr)i_0.
\end{aligned}\tag{8.28}
In particular,
The second term in $d_2$ is the contribution of the first correction to the representative.
To see it directly, take $\mathcal O_0=i_0i_1a$ with $a\in E_2$, and choose $\mathcal O_1=-h_0Q_1\mathcal O_0$.
Then

\begin{aligned}
Q_0\mathcal O_1
&=-(1-i_0\pi_0)Q_1\mathcal O_0=-Q_1\mathcal O_0,\\
Q_0(Q_2\mathcal O_0+Q_1\mathcal O_1)
&=-Q_1^2\mathcal O_0-Q_1Q_0\mathcal O_1=0,\\
\pi_1\pi_0(Q_2\mathcal O_0+Q_1\mathcal O_1)&=d_2a.
\end{aligned}\tag{8.30}
Equivalently, with $[\cdot]_r$ denoting a class on $E_r$,

d_2[\mathcal O_0]_2
=[Q_2\mathcal O_0+Q_1\mathcal O_1]_2.\tag{8.31}
Changing $\mathcal O_1$ by a classical cocycle changes the projected obstruction by a $d_1$ boundary.
Corrected representatives.
For a class $a\in E_3$, the vanishing of $d_2i_2a$ determines corrections through two loops.
One choice requiring only $Q_0,Q_1,Q_2$ is

\begin{aligned}
\mathcal O_0&=i_0i_1i_2a,\\
\mathcal O_1
&=-h_0Q_1\mathcal O_0
-i_0h_1\pi_0(Q_2-Q_1h_0Q_1)\mathcal O_0,\\
\mathcal O_2&=-h_0(Q_2\mathcal O_0+Q_1\mathcal O_1).
\end{aligned}\tag{8.32}
Indeed,
The term with $h_1d_1$ vanishes by the coefficient of $\hbar$ in $(\mathbf Q^{(1)})^2=0$.
Equation (8.24) then verifies all three closure equations in (8.21).
At every page the same construction gives

For $a\in E_{r+1}$, choose $\mathcal O_s$ as the coefficient of $\hbar^s$ in $i_0(\hbar)\cdots i_{r-1}(\hbar)i_ra$.

The transfer incorporates the higher corrections into $d_r$; kernels, images, linear independence and product relations can then be computed on the corresponding subquotients of classical representatives.
Higher differentials on the graviton part.
Applying the projection identity in [(8.27)](#eq-page-transfer-identities) on successive pages gives

\pi_{r-1}(\hbar)\cdots\pi_0(\hbar)\,\mathbf Q
=\hbar^r\,\mathbf Q^{(r)}\,\pi_{r-1}(\hbar)\cdots\pi_0(\hbar).\tag{8.38}
If $\mathbf Q\mathcal O=0$, dividing (8.38) applied to $\mathcal O$ by $\hbar^r$ gives $\mathbf Q^{(r)}\pi_{r-1}(\hbar)\cdots\pi_0(\hbar)\mathcal O=0$.
Its constant term is $d_r\pi_{r-1}\cdots\pi_0\mathcal O_0$, and by induction on $r$ the projection $\pi_{r-1}\cdots\pi_0\mathcal O_0$ is the class $[\mathcal O_0]_r$.
Hence a class with a closed completion satisfies
d_r[\mathcal O_0]_r=0\qquad(r\ge1).\tag{8.39}
By Theorem 8.1, every $d_r$ with $r\ge1$ vanishes on the graviton part.

On classes of cohomological degree $k$, the rank of $d_r$ is the dimension of the space of degree-$k$ classical classes that survive to $E_r$, including those that vanish there, modulo those that survive to $E_{r+1}$.
Every class of the graviton part survives to every page.
In each charge sector, the ranks of all $d_r$ with $r\ge1$ on degree $k$ therefore add up to at most the number of fortuitous classes of degree $k$.
These classes are sparse among the classical classes known so far [20; 18], so the successive differentials are extremely sparse on the known cohomology.
A closed completion can become a quantum coboundary.
For completed operators satisfying

\mathbf Q X=\hbar^r\mathcal O,\qquad
\mathbf Q\mathcal O=0,
\qquad
\mathcal O=\mathbf Q(\hbar^{-r}X),\tag{8.40}
the last equality holds after inverting $\hbar$.
Over formal power series, the first equality records a class annihilated by $\hbar^r$.
The successive pages record these $d_r$-exact classes at their respective orders in $\hbar$.

In each cohomological degree, expand the gauge-invariant local operators in a basis of component fields and holomorphic derivatives, imposing the graded field relations and the trace identities at that rank.

The input on $E_r$ is a basis of representatives in each degree, completed through order $r-1$ by $i_0(\hbar)\cdots i_{r-1}(\hbar)$, together with the matrix of $d_r$ from (8.25).
The output is a contraction $(i_r,\pi_r,h_r)$, hence $E_{r+1}$, the matrix of $d_{r+1}$ and the next corrections.
Let $d_r^k:E_r^k\to E_r^{k+1}$ denote the differential in cohomological degree $k$.
Choose the columns of $B_r^k$ to span $\operatorname{im}d_r^{k-1}$, extend them by the columns of $H_r^k$ to a basis of $\ker d_r^k$, and choose $L_r^k$ so that

d_r^kL_r^k=B_r^{k+1},\qquad
(B_r^k\;H_r^k\;L_r^k)\ \text{is invertible}.\tag{8.41}

Here the block $1$ is the identity on the indicated group of columns.
Thus
The inclusion $i_r$ is the natural embedding of the chosen representatives.
The freedom lies in the complements $H_r^k$ and $L_r^k$, which fix $\pi_r$ and $h_r$.
Three choices are typical.

In the pivot splitting, used in the calculations of Section 9, the monomials are ordered and the columns of $d_r^k$ are eliminated in exact rational arithmetic, the first monomial of each reduced column being its pivot.

The basis vectors whose images supply new pivots form $L_r^k$, and their images form $B_r^{k+1}$; the linear dependencies found in the elimination span $\ker d_r^k$, and the kernel vectors independent modulo $B_r^k$ form $H_r^k$.

Then $\pi_r$ reduces a vector against the pivot columns of $(B_r^k\;H_r^k\;L_r^k)$ and keeps its $H_r^k$ coordinates, and $h_r$ replaces its $B_r^k$ coordinates by the same combination of the preimages $L_r^{k-1}$.

For the largest sectors the pivot columns can be selected modulo a prime after a random linear projection of the rows; the coefficients are then recomputed over $\mathbb Q$ on the selected columns, and the result is checked by applying $Q_0$ exactly.

In the orthogonal splitting, with the monomials orthonormal, $H_r^k=\ker d_r^k\cap(\operatorname{im}d_r^{k-1})^\perp$, $\pi_r$ is the orthogonal projection, and $h_r$ is the Moore–Penrose pseudoinverse of $d_r$; it does not depend on an ordering of the monomials, but its matrices are dense.

When a pair of letters decouples from the others under $Q_0$, as $Q_0\beta^s=-m\gamma_s'$ and $Q_0\gamma_s'=0$ in the shifted fields [(9.2)](#eq-massshift) of Section [9.1](#sec-SQEDlift), the homotopy of that pair has a closed form: the odd derivation that replaces each factor $\gamma_s'$, with its derivatives, by the same derivative of $-\beta^s/m$, divided by the number of letters $\gamma_s',\beta^s$; the projection sets these letters to zero.
Two contractions $(i_r,\pi_r,h_r)$ and $(i_r',\pi_r',h_r')$ of the same page give conjugate transferred differentials.
By (8.27),

The pages, the ranks of all $d_s$, and the vanishing of a given class are therefore independent of the choices.
At each step, check the nilpotence of the transferred differential and its intertwining identity with $i_r(\hbar)$ through the retained order in $\hbar$.
In practice $\pi_r$ and $h_r$ are applied by reduction against the stored pivot columns rather than formed as matrices.

The algorithm does not require the quantum product.

On every page the class of $A\star B$, whose leading term is $A_0B_0$, is $[A_0]_r[B_0]_r=[A_0B_0]_r$ by (8.37): products of classes are obtained by multiplying classical representatives and reducing on $E_r$, and $d_r$ acts on them by the Leibniz rule.
Derivative grading.
A monomial has two holomorphic derivative totals: its numbers of $\partial_{+\dot+}$ and $\partial_{+\dot-}$ derivatives.
Every current is linear in the injected currents, and the current form in (B.21) has degree $n$ in each dotted component.
For each fixed $\dot a$ the kernel of an $n$-loop graph therefore satisfies

Powers of $\lambda_{v,+\dot a}$ become derivatives of output letters and powers of $z_e^{+\dot a}$ remove input derivatives, so each $Q_n$ adds $n$ derivatives in each holomorphic direction, as observed for pure gauge theory in [6, Equations (3.44)–(3.45)].
The classical differential $Q_0$ preserves both totals, and the contractions $(i_r,\pi_r,h_r)$ can be chosen homogeneous.
By (8.25), every term of $d_r$ then adds $r$ derivatives in each direction.
Lemma 8.2.
A class can be $d_r$-exact only if both derivative totals of its leading representative are at least $r$.
In particular, a class whose leading representative has no holomorphic derivatives is $d_r$-exact for no $r\ge1$.
Proof.
A preimage under $d_r$ would have both totals lowered by $r$, and they must be nonnegative.

The $n$ loop currents of each dotted component are linear in the injected currents, which act as derivatives on the output letters; a differential on the $r$th page therefore raises each derivative total by $r$, and a class without derivatives cannot be its image.
9 Tests of lifting beyond one loop
The obstruction equations of Section 8 decide whether loop corrections beyond one loop lift classes that survive the one-loop differential, a question left open in [16, Section 1].

A classical cocycle survives at every perturbative order if it is not classically exact and admits a closed completion that is a quantum coboundary at no positive loop order; by Lemma 8.2, the last condition holds for a leading representative without holomorphic derivatives.
In massive SQED the answer is positive: Section 9.1 exhibits a class that survives one loop and is lifted at two loops.
Every other class we test survives at every perturbative order.
In the complete low-letter sectors of $\mathcal N=4$ $SU(2)$ and $SU(3)$ theory treated in Section 9.2, every classical class is a multi-graviton completed by Theorem 8.1.

Section 9.3 completes the threshold fortuitous class of $\mathcal N=4$ $SU(2)$ theory, which this theorem does not cover, together with its graviton-dressed descendants; for the descendant carrying holomorphic derivatives, an explicit calculation excludes $d_1$-exactness.
Section 9.4 completes a graviton square and a non-graviton class of a quartic deformation with the spider kernels.
9.1 A two-loop lifting example: massive SQED with a cubic superpotential
Consider a $U(1)$ gauge theory with two chiral multiplets of charges $+1,-1$ and a neutral chiral multiplet.
Its interaction is
\mathcal I=ig\mathsf c(\gamma_+\beta^+-\gamma_-\beta^-)+\frac m2\gamma_s^2+y\gamma_s\gamma_+\gamma_-,\qquad my\ne0,\tag{9.1}
Here $m$ is the mass of the neutral multiplet and $y$ is the cubic superpotential coefficient.
We exhibit a gauge-invariant cocycle $\mathcal O_0$ that survives the one-loop differential and has the nonzero second obstruction (9.14).

The calculation has five steps: the exact elimination of the massive pair, the source and its classical closure, the one-loop action and a first correction, the combined second-order residual, and its class in the finite obstruction quotient.
The massive pair.
The neutral mass can be included exactly before computing the obstruction quotient.
In the twisted BV complex, a canonical change of fields isolates a massive pair.
The shifts
complete the square and preserve the cotangent pairing:

\frac m2\gamma_s^2+y\gamma_s\gamma_+\gamma_-
=\frac m2(\gamma_s')^2-\frac{y^2}{2m}(\gamma_+\gamma_-)^2.\tag{9.3}
The pair $Q_0\beta^s=-m\gamma_s'$, $Q_0\gamma_s'=0$ is contractible.
The exact classical effective superpotential is

\bar W_{\mathrm{eff}}=-\frac{y^2}{2m}(\gamma_+\gamma_-)^2,
\qquad\bar W_{\mathrm{eff}}^{++--}=-\frac{2y^2}{m}.\tag{9.4}
The superscript $++--$ denotes two derivatives with respect to each of $\gamma_+$ and $\gamma_-$.
In the transfer formula below, $Q_n$ is expressed in the shifted fields before eliminating the massive pair.

The second example is the flavour-singlet class $\mathcal O_{16}$ of [19, Eq. (4.53)].
Its subscript records its field weight sixteen.

Its preimage would require a flavour singlet of type $\beta^4\mathsf b$, and the $SU(2)$ invariant contractions of these letters contain no such singlet [19, Section 4.4].

Solving the four representative equations gives, for $M\ne0$,

\mathcal O[\mathcal O_{16}]=\sum_{r=0}^4\hbar^r\mathcal O_r[\mathcal O_{16}],
\qquad

\quad(0\le r\le4).\tag{9.44}
The coefficient archive gives the four corrections and their exact polynomial identities, with the powers of $M$ fixed term by term by the graph contractions.
The coefficients have weights $16-4r$.
A four-loop operation contracts at most five input letters and lowers their combined weight by $16$.

At order $r\ge5$ the whole closure equation has weight $16-4r<0$.

10 Conclusion
Within the holomorphic graph-integral framework of Wang and the operatope [7; 8], the evaluated graph kernels give the loop-corrected supercharge and quantum multiplication on BPS cohomology.

Reading the operatope current equations as those of an electrical network, and reversing iterated series and parallel reductions as a change of variables on Schwinger space, turns each fan, spider and book kernel into a polynomial integral in positive coordinates over products of intervals and simplices: the spanning-tree denominators of the Schwinger integrand [7] cancel, and every Taylor coefficient is a finite factorial sum.

For these type I$'$ graphs, polynomial integrals over unit cubes had been obtained by recursion in [14, Theorem 4.13]; the reduction derives positive coordinates from the Schwinger integral itself, gives closed forms at every loop order, and, through zero-source star–triangle moves, also reaches the marked graphs not of type I$'$ that occur in the quantum product for cubic interactions.
In $\mathcal N=4$ Yang–Mills theory, (7.3) gives the supercharge at every loop order, including its action on arbitrary holomorphic derivatives, and reduces at one loop to the operator of [16].

The graviton part of the classical cohomology is therefore completed at once; every successive differential vanishes on it, and a completed class is lifted exactly when it becomes a quantum coboundary.
In massive SQED with quadratic and cubic superpotential terms, the class (9.6) survives the one-loop equation and has the nonzero second obstruction (9.14).
This example shows that higher-loop corrections change the cohomology after the one-loop differential has acted, answering for this theory the question raised in [16, Section 1].
In $\mathcal N=4$ $SU(2)$ theory, the threshold fortuitous class and its three graviton-dressed descendants admit closed quantum completions and survive at every perturbative order.
The quartic deformation supplies further examples whose completions terminate by weight.
We must warn the reader about the setting in which these results are derived.

All calculations are performed in the holomorphically twisted theory, whose graph integrals are ultraviolet finite [7, Theorem 5, Corollary 4]; for this reason neither the action nor the local holomorphic composite operators studied here require counterterms [8, Section 1], [16, footnote 22].
Several facts support the twisted calculation, among them the agreement of the one-loop operator with the Konishi anomaly [2; 3; 16].

No proof exists, however, that the corresponding calculation in the untwisted theory, which is considerably more complicated and not yet fully defined, gives the same loop-corrected supersymmetry transformations and products.
We regard this comparison as a valuable direction.
It meets a problem that is, perhaps surprisingly, still open: an exact regularization and renormalization of supersymmetric gauge theory.
Dimensional regularization, the most effective tool for gauge theories, has persistent difficulties with supersymmetry, whose chiral structure depends on four dimensions [9; 10; 11; 12; 13].

No modified dimensional scheme has been proved to preserve gauge symmetry and supersymmetry simultaneously, so that the Slavnov–Taylor identities hold automatically, while capturing the chiral anomaly correctly and consistently.

Gauge-covariant heat-kernel methods in superspace background fields have been proposed; they do not yet treat one-loop contributions cleanly, involve subtleties such as Pauli–Villars pairs, and either leave the regularization and renormalization of composite operators with matter components unresolved or give up BRST symmetry.
Other methods require far heavier calculations, often fail to preserve gauge symmetry automatically, and produce an unusually rich counterterm structure.

A further study of the BV formalism developed by Costello [5] may give valuable insight into how symmetries are protected, and how symmetry algebras are realized, in perturbative supersymmetric gauge theory, a question that looks basic and is still far from settled.

Let $\Gamma$ be a marked Laman graph whose interaction subgraph is an interaction forest as above.

The column of a resistor in the Jacobian numerator has entries only in the rows of its interaction end nodes: scaling its conductance at fixed node potentials changes the current fed into each end node by $\pm$ its own current.

A nonzero term lets every interaction node take up two resistors, one per dotted component; in a forest this sharing is unique: a spoke goes to its interaction node, and an internal resistor to the side of the tree that is one resistor short (Figure 31).

Theorem B.3 (Star–triangle move).
Let the node $v$ of a Laman circuit $\Gamma$ carry no source and exactly three resistors, to $u$, $w$ and $x$, and let resistors join $x$ to $u$ and to $w$.
Orient $vu,vw,vx$ away from $v$ and $ux,wx$ towards $x$, and order the resistors of $\Gamma$ with $vu,vw,vx$ first.

The star–triangle move (B.82) at $v$, followed by the parallel merges of the new resistors on $ux$ and $wx$ with the old ones (B.31), leaves the circuit $\Gamma^{\mathrm{red}}$: the new resistor $uw$ first, the merged resistors in place of $ux$ and $wx$, the remaining resistors in their order, and the sources of $\Gamma$.
With $r_1$ and $r_2$ the fractions of the merged currents on $ux$ and $wx$ carried by the old resistors,

\mathcal I^{\mathrm{raw\ cut}}_\Gamma(\lambda;z)
=\int_0^1\!dr_1\int_0^1\!dr_2\;r_1r_2\,
\bigl(y^{\mathrm{red}}_{ux,+\dot a}\,y^{\mathrm{red}}_{wx,+}{}^{\dot a}\bigr)\,
\mathcal I^{\mathrm{raw\ cut}}_{\Gamma^{\mathrm{red}}}\bigl(\lambda;z^{\mathrm{red}}\bigr),\tag{B.33}

z^{\mathrm{red}}_{uw}=z_{vw}-z_{vu},\qquad
z^{\mathrm{red}}_{ux}=r_1z_{ux}+(1-r_1)(z_{vx}-z_{vu}),\qquad
z^{\mathrm{red}}_{wx}=r_2z_{wx}+(1-r_2)(z_{vx}-z_{vw}),
and $z^{\mathrm{red}}_e=z_e$ for the other resistors.
Proof.
Resistances.
The star–triangle move maps the three resistances at $v$ bijectively to the three sides of the triangle on $u,w,x$ (B.82).
The merges give the old resistances $t_{ux}=t^{\mathrm{red}}_{ux}/r_1$, $t_{wx}=t^{\mathrm{red}}_{wx}/r_2$ and the new sides $t^{\mathrm{red}}_{ux}/(1-r_1)$, $t^{\mathrm{red}}_{wx}/(1-r_2)$.
The resistance ratios of $\Gamma$ are therefore $(r_1,r_2)\in(0,1)^2$ together with those of $\Gamma^{\mathrm{red}}$.

The Jacobian of the five old resistances with respect to $(r_1,r_2,t^{\mathrm{red}}_{uw},t^{\mathrm{red}}_{ux},t^{\mathrm{red}}_{wx})$ is negative, so with the stated orders $\eta_\Gamma$ is a negative multiple of $dr_1\wedge dr_2\wedge\eta_{\Gamma^{\mathrm{red}}}$.
Currents.
Outside the star and the two merged resistors the currents of $\Gamma$ and $\Gamma^{\mathrm{red}}$ agree.
The old resistors carry $y_{ux}=r_1y^{\mathrm{red}}_{ux}$ and $y_{wx}=r_2y^{\mathrm{red}}_{wx}$, the new sides the rest, and by (B.82) the star carries

y_{vu}=-y^{\mathrm{red}}_{uw}-(1-r_1)y^{\mathrm{red}}_{ux},\qquad
y_{vw}=y^{\mathrm{red}}_{uw}-(1-r_2)y^{\mathrm{red}}_{wx},\qquad
y_{vx}=(1-r_1)y^{\mathrm{red}}_{ux}+(1-r_2)y^{\mathrm{red}}_{wx}.
Displacements.

Substituting these currents gives $\sum_ez_e^{+\dot a}y_{e,+\dot a}=\sum_ez^{\mathrm{red},+\dot a}_ey^{\mathrm{red}}_{e,+\dot a}$ with the stated $z^{\mathrm{red}}$: each merged current divides between the old resistor and the path through $v$.
Loop currents.
$\Gamma$ has one loop more than $\Gamma^{\mathrm{red}}$.
Take as loop currents of $\Gamma$ those through the old resistors $ux$ and $wx$ together with the loop currents of $\Gamma^{\mathrm{red}}$ other than the one through the new resistor $uw$.
Modulo the differentials of the latter, $dy^{\mathrm{red}}_{ux}\equiv-dy^{\mathrm{red}}_{uw}$ and $dy^{\mathrm{red}}_{wx}\equiv dy^{\mathrm{red}}_{uw}$, and

the two old resistors carry the fractions $r_1$ and $r_2$ of the merged currents, and as these fractions vary their currents sweep the area spanned by $r_1y^{\mathrm{red}}_{ux}$ and $r_2y^{\mathrm{red}}_{wx}$, while the loop through the new resistor supplies the rest of the current form of $\Gamma^{\mathrm{red}}$.
Orientation.
The negative signs of the Jacobian and of the area element cancel, which gives (B.33).

When $x$ is joined to only one of $u$ and $w$, the star–triangle move leaves one resistor too many: in a cubic product forest this happens at the first of two leaves hanging from a node without spokes.
The moves at the two leaves then form one step, which removes two loops.
Theorem B.4 (Star–triangle moves at two leaves).
Let the nodes $v_1,v_2$ of a Laman circuit $\Gamma$ carry no source and exactly three resistors each, to $u$, $A$ and $B$, where $A$ and $B$ are joined and $u$ is joined to neither.
Orient the six resistors at $v_1,v_2$ away from $v_1,v_2$ and $AB$ from $A$ to $B$, and order the resistors of $\Gamma$ as $v_1u,v_1A,v_1B,v_2u,v_2A,v_2B$, followed by the others.

The star–triangle moves at $v_1$ and $v_2$ and the parallel merges of the new resistors leave the circuit $\Gamma^{\mathrm{red}}$: the new resistors $uA,uB$ first, the merged resistor in place of $AB$, the remaining resistors in their order, and the sources of $\Gamma$.

Let $r_1$ and $r_2$ be the fractions of the merged currents on $uA$ and $uB$ carried by the sides from $v_1$, and $r_3$, $r_4$ and $1-r_3-r_4$ the fractions of the merged current on $AB$ carried by the sides from $v_1$, from $v_2$ and by the old resistor.
Then

\begin{aligned}
\mathcal I^{\mathrm{raw\ cut}}_\Gamma(\lambda;z)
={}&\int_0^1\!dr_1\int_0^1\!dr_2\int_{r_3+r_4<1}\!dr_3\,dr_4\;(r_1-r_2)(1-r_3-r_4)\\
&\times\bigl(y^{\mathrm{red}}_{uA,+\dot a}\,y^{\mathrm{red}}_{AB,+}{}^{\dot a}\bigr)
\bigl(y^{\mathrm{red}}_{uB,+\dot b}\,y^{\mathrm{red}}_{AB,+}{}^{\dot b}\bigr)\,
\mathcal I^{\mathrm{raw\ cut}}_{\Gamma^{\mathrm{red}}}\bigl(\lambda;z^{\mathrm{red}}\bigr),
\end{aligned}\tag{B.34}
and $z^{\mathrm{red}}_e=z_e$ for the other resistors.
Proof.
Resistances.

The two star–triangle moves are bijections onto the sides of two triangles on $u,A,B$, and the merges give the pieces of $uA$, $uB$ and $AB$ the resistances $t^{\mathrm{red}}$ divided by their fractions.

The resistance ratios of $\Gamma$ are $(r_1,r_2)\in(0,1)^2$, $(r_3,r_4)$ in the simplex, and those of $\Gamma^{\mathrm{red}}$; the Jacobian of the seven old resistances with respect to $(r_1,\ldots,r_4,t^{\mathrm{red}}_{uA},t^{\mathrm{red}}_{uB},t^{\mathrm{red}}_{AB})$ is positive, so with the stated orders $\eta_\Gamma$ is a positive multiple of $dr_1\wedge\cdots\wedge dr_4\wedge\eta_{\Gamma^{\mathrm{red}}}$.
Currents and displacements.
By (B.82) the two stars carry

\begin{aligned}
y_{v_1u}&=-r_1y^{\mathrm{red}}_{uA}-r_2y^{\mathrm{red}}_{uB},&
y_{v_2u}&=-(1-r_1)y^{\mathrm{red}}_{uA}-(1-r_2)y^{\mathrm{red}}_{uB},\\
y_{v_1A}&=r_1y^{\mathrm{red}}_{uA}-r_3y^{\mathrm{red}}_{AB},&
y_{v_2A}&=(1-r_1)y^{\mathrm{red}}_{uA}-r_4y^{\mathrm{red}}_{AB},\\
y_{v_1B}&=r_2y^{\mathrm{red}}_{uB}+r_3y^{\mathrm{red}}_{AB},&
y_{v_2B}&=(1-r_2)y^{\mathrm{red}}_{uB}+r_4y^{\mathrm{red}}_{AB},
\end{aligned}
and the old resistor $AB$ carries $(1-r_3-r_4)y^{\mathrm{red}}_{AB}$; substituting gives the stated $z^{\mathrm{red}}$.
Loop currents.
$\Gamma$ has two loops more than $\Gamma^{\mathrm{red}}$.
Take as loop currents of $\Gamma$ those through $AB$, $v_1B$ and $v_2A$ together with the loop currents of $\Gamma^{\mathrm{red}}$ other than the one through $AB$.

Modulo the differentials of the latter, $dy^{\mathrm{red}}_{uA}\equiv dy^{\mathrm{red}}_{AB}$ and $dy^{\mathrm{red}}_{uB}\equiv-dy^{\mathrm{red}}_{AB}$, and the three currents $(1-r_3-r_4)y^{\mathrm{red}}_{AB}$, $y_{v_1B}$, $y_{v_2A}$ depend on $r_1,\ldots,r_4$ and on $y^{\mathrm{red}}_{AB}$ alone.
Their Jacobian determinant is
(r_1-r_2)(1-r_3-r_4)\bigl(y^{\mathrm{red}}_{uA}\,y^{\mathrm{red}}_{AB}\bigr)\bigl(y^{\mathrm{red}}_{uB}\,y^{\mathrm{red}}_{AB}\bigr),

and with the factors $-dy_{+\dot+}\wedge dy_{+\dot-}$ the area elements of the three loops give this determinant times $dr_1\wedge\cdots\wedge dr_4\wedge\bigl(-dy^{\mathrm{red}}_{AB,+\dot+}\wedge dy^{\mathrm{red}}_{AB,+\dot-}\bigr)$.
Orientation.
Both signs are positive, which gives (B.34).

B.10 Spider arms: reduction and reconstruction
Order of the reduction.
The arms meet only at $A$ and $B$, so they are reduced one at a time, in any order (Figure 38).
Along arm $i$ the vertices $v_{i,1},\ldots,v_{i,\ell_i-1}$ are eliminated in turn.

Before its elimination, $v_{i,j}$ keeps two resistors, the arm resistor to $v_{i,j+1}$ and its reduced spoke to $B$; a series step joins them, passing the fraction $r_{i,2j-1}$ of its source to $v_{i,j+1}$ and the rest to $B$, and a parallel merge combines the result with the spoke $v_{i,j+1}B$, the new resistor carrying the fraction $r_{i,2j}$ of the merged current (Figure 39).

The last vertex $v_{i,\ell_i}$ is joined to $A$ and $B$; its series step passes the fraction $r_{i,2\ell_i-1}$ of its source to $A$ and leaves one resistor between $A$ and $B$, of resistance $1/r_{i,2\ell_i}$.

When every arm has been reduced, the $a$ arm resistors and the original resistor $AB$ are in parallel, and one merge leaves the unit resistor (B.63), in which arm $i$ carries the share $r_{i,2\ell_i}$.
Merging each arm resistor with $AB$ as soon as it appears, as in Figure 18, gives the same final resistor and the same shares.

B.13 Graphs of type I$'$
A graph is of type I$'$ [14, Definition 4.12] if it is built from one edge by repeatedly adding a vertex joined to the two endpoints of an existing edge.
Theorem B.2 reverses each construction step, so such graphs are reduced to that edge by series–parallel moves alone.
Proposition B.5 (Spiders and graphs of type I$'$).
Let $\Gamma$ consist of the edge $AB$, a forest of trees $T_j$, and at most one spoke from each interaction vertex to each insertion, with $|E_j|=|T_j|+1$.
(i) $\Gamma$ is of type I$'$ if and only if the two endpoints of every internal edge are joined to a common insertion.

(ii) For cubic interactions, $\Gamma$ is of type I$'$ if and only if every tree is a path $v_{i,1}-v_{i,2}-\cdots-v_{i,\ell_i}$, an arm, all of whose vertices are joined to the same insertion, with $v_{i,1}$ the degree-two vertex and $v_{i,\ell_i}$ joined to both insertions.
For $n\ge3$, $\Gamma$ is a spider (Definition 6.4) if and only if it is of type I$'$ and all arms with $\ell_i\ge2$ are joined to the same insertion.

Graphs not of type I$'$ first occur at $n=3$; graphs of type I$'$ that are not spiders, and trees with a vertex of tree degree three, first occur at $n=4$.
Proof.
(i) Each construction step wires a new node by two resistors to the two ends of an existing resistor, so in a circuit of type I$'$ with at least three nodes every resistor closes a triangle.
For an internal resistor $uv$ the third node of its triangle is wired to $u$ and to $v$; an interaction node would close a loop of internal resistors in $T_j$, so the third node is $A$ or $B$.
Conversely, assume the condition and induct on $n$; for $n=0$, $\Gamma$ is the marked resistor $AB$.
A tree with a single node is wired to $A$ and $B$ by its two spokes, which are in series across $AB$.
Otherwise let $T_j$ have $|T_j|\ge2$ nodes and $L\ge2$ end nodes.
Every node of $T_j$ lies on an internal resistor and therefore has a spoke.

If every end node had two spokes, $T_j$ would have $|E_j|\ge2L+(|T_j|-L)\ge|T_j|+2$ spokes; some end node therefore has exactly one spoke, to $X\in\{A,B\}$, and its neighbour in $T_j$ is also wired to $X$.
In both cases the node has two resistors in series across an existing resistor, and removing it reverses one construction step.
(ii) A node of tree degree three has no spoke by (6.5), and neither has the node with two resistors when both are internal; their internal resistors violate the condition of (i).

blocks.source: Order of the reduction.
The trees meet only at $A$ and $B$ and are reduced one at a time (Figure 45).

In each tree the source-free trivalent vertices are removed by star–triangle reductions, each after all the vertices of its subtree: such a vertex $v$, with tree neighbour $u$ towards the root, then has the neighbours $u,A,B$, and the triangle $uA,uB,AB$ that replaces it merges in parallel with the resistors already there.
A vertex whose subtrees are gone becomes a leaf in turn, and the tree shrinks to its root, the degree-two vertex with the source, joined to $A$ and $B$.
A series reduction at every root leaves one resistor per tree between $A$ and $B$, and one parallel merge with $AB$ leaves the unit resistor, as for spiders (Figure 38).

In kernel form, a leaf whose tree neighbour keeps a spoke is removed by Theorem B.3, two leaves at a vertex without spokes by Theorem B.4, and every root by Theorem B.2, each step integrating the kernel of the smaller circuit.

Lemma B.8 (Closed current form).
For an almost-Laman network the integrand of (B.92) is a closed form of degree $\dim\mathbb{RP}^{|\Gamma_1|-1}_{>0}-1$.

blocks.source: Zooming into a short.
For every $\emptyset\ne\gamma\subseteq\Gamma_1$ record the resistance ratios inside $\gamma$, $\bigl(t_e/\sum_{h\in\gamma}t_h\bigr)_{e\in\gamma}$, a point of a closed simplex.

The closure of $\mathbb{RP}^{|\Gamma_1|-1}_{>0}$ in the product of these simplices is compact; it is the compactified Schwinger space modulo rescaling, $\widehat{(0,+\infty)^{|\Gamma_1|}}/\mathbb R_+$, of [7, Definition 13, Remark 8, Proposition 7].
A flag $\emptyset=\gamma_0\subsetneq\gamma_1\subsetneq\cdots\subsetneq\gamma_m\subsetneq\gamma_{m+1}=\Gamma_1$ gives the chart

t_e=s_is_{i+1}\cdots s_m\,r_e\quad(e\in\gamma_i\setminus\gamma_{i-1}),\qquad
\sum_{e\in\gamma_i\setminus\gamma_{i-1}}r_e=1,\qquad s\in[0,\infty)^m,\tag{B.94}
with $r$ in the product of open simplices: at $s_i=0$ the resistors of $\gamma_i$ shrink infinitely faster than those of $\gamma_{i+1}\setminus\gamma_i$, a short inside a short.

Every recorded ratio is a quotient of polynomials in $(s,r)$ with nonnegative coefficients, its denominator containing $\sum_{h\in\gamma\cap(\gamma_i\setminus\gamma_{i-1})}r_h$, with $\gamma_i\setminus\gamma_{i-1}$ the least shrunk layer meeting $\gamma$, hence positive; $r_e$ and $s_i$ are quotients of recorded ratios.
These charts cover the closure (order the resistances by the rate at which they shrink) and make it a manifold with corners.
Its faces of codimension one are the flags with $m=1$, one for each $\emptyset\ne\gamma\subsetneq\Gamma_1$:

\{s=0\}=\mathbb{RP}^{|\gamma|-1}_{>0}\times\mathbb{RP}^{|\Gamma_1\setminus\gamma|-1}_{>0},
\qquad s=\frac{\sum_{e\in\gamma}t_e}{\sum_{e\notin\gamma}t_e},\tag{B.95}
the ratios inside the short times the ratios of the remaining resistors (Figure [49](#fig-short-zoom)).

For $\gamma\subseteq\Gamma_1$ the islands are the connected components of $(\Gamma_0,\gamma)$ that contain resistors, $c(\gamma)$ is the number of components of $(\Gamma_0,\gamma)$ and $h_1(\gamma)=|\gamma|-|\Gamma_0|+c(\gamma)$.

The shorted network $\Gamma/\gamma$ has the components of $(\Gamma_0,\gamma)$ as nodes, each carrying the sum of its sources, and the resistors $\Gamma_1\setminus\gamma$; a resistor with both terminals in one island is a self-loop of $\Gamma/\gamma$.

Proof.
For a spanning tree $T$, $T\cap\gamma_i$ is a forest in $(\Gamma_0,\gamma_i)$, so

\prod_{h\in\Gamma_1\setminus T}t_h=\prod_{i=1}^{m}s_i^{\,|\gamma_i\setminus T|}\prod_{h\in\Gamma_1\setminus T}r_h,
\qquad
|\gamma_i\setminus T|\ge|\gamma_i|-|\Gamma_0|+c(\gamma_i)=h_1(\gamma_i),

with equality for every $i$ if and only if each $T\cap\gamma_i$ spans $(\Gamma_0,\gamma_i)$, that is, $T=B_1\sqcup\cdots\sqcup B_{m+1}$ with $B_i$ a maximal spanning forest of $\gamma_i/\gamma_{i-1}$.
The dominant spanning trees omit as few shorted resistors as possible: each contains a spanning tree of every island and, outside the islands, a spanning tree of the shorted network (Figure 50).
By Lemma B.9 the currents (B.22) are quotients of polynomials in $(s,r)$ with denominators positive on every chart.
They extend smoothly to $\widehat{(0,+\infty)^{|\Gamma_1|}}/\mathbb R_+$, and so does the integrand of (B.92), closed by continuity.

blocks.source: Lemma B.10 (Currents on a short).
On the face (B.95):

(i) the resistors of $\Gamma_1\setminus\gamma$ carry the currents of the shorted network $\Gamma/\gamma$ with resistances $r_{\Gamma_1\setminus\gamma}$; a resistor joining two terminals of one island is bypassed by the short and carries no current;
(ii) the resistors of $\gamma$ carry the currents of the islands with resistances $r_\gamma$, fed at $v$ by
its own source, minus the current the outer resistors carry away from $v$, plus the current they deliver to $v$ (Figure 49(b)).
On each island these sources sum to zero.
Proof.
With $t_e=s\,r_e$ ($e\in\gamma$) and $t_e=r_e$ ($e\notin\gamma$), the voltage law (3.8) around a cycle $C$ of $\Gamma$ reads
\sum_{e\in C\setminus\gamma}\pm r_ey_{e,+\dot a}+s\sum_{e\in C\cap\gamma}\pm r_ey_{e,+\dot a}=0 .
At $s=0$ the voltage drops across the islands disappear (Figure 51(a)).

Every cycle of $\Gamma/\gamma$ lifts to a cycle of $\Gamma$ through paths in the islands, so the outer currents obey the voltage law of $\Gamma/\gamma$; a self-loop $f$ of $\Gamma/\gamma$, closed by a path in its island, gives $r_fy_f=0$ (Figure 51(b)).

Summing (B.20) over the nodes of one component of $(\Gamma_0,\gamma)$ cancels the island currents and gives the current law of $\Gamma/\gamma$ at that node, which also makes the $\lambda^\gamma_v$ sum to zero on each island.

For a cycle $C\subseteq\gamma$ the relation is $s\sum_{e\in C}\pm r_ey_e=0$; dividing by $s>0$ and letting $s\to0$, the island currents obey the voltage law of the islands with resistances $r_\gamma$, and (B.20) at $v$ is the current law of the islands with the sources $\lambda^\gamma_v$ (Figure 51(c)).
The limits exist by Lemma B.9; uniqueness of the network solutions gives (i) and (ii).

blocks.source: Lemma B.11 (Island and outer network).
Let $T=B\sqcup T'$, with $B$ a maximal spanning forest of $(\Gamma_0,\gamma)$ and $T'$ a spanning tree of $\Gamma/\gamma$.
On the face (B.95),
with $d_\gamma$ the differential along $\mathbb{RP}^{|\gamma|-1}_{>0}$ at fixed outer ratios.
The first factor is the current form of the islands at the sources $\lambda^\gamma$, the second the current form of $\Gamma/\gamma$.
Proof.
The chords of $T$ are $(\gamma\setminus B)\sqcup((\Gamma_1\setminus\gamma)\setminus T')$ (Figure 52).
By Lemma B.10 the outer currents depend only on the outer ratios, and for $e\in\gamma$

dy_e=d_\gamma y_e+\sum_{v}\frac{\partial y_e}{\partial\lambda^\gamma_v}\,d\lambda^\gamma_v,
\qquad
d\lambda^\gamma_v\in\operatorname{span}\{dy_f:f\notin\gamma\}=\operatorname{span}\{dy_c:c\in(\Gamma_1\setminus\gamma)\setminus T'\},
since the tree currents of $T'$ are affine in the chord currents of $\Gamma/\gamma$.

The island learns about the outer network only through the currents delivered to it, and all $2h_1(\Gamma/\gamma)$ one-forms along which these move occur in the second factor, so the terms with $d\lambda^\gamma$ drop out.

blocks.source: Proposition B.12 (Contributing shorts).
Let $\Gamma$ be almost Laman.
The integrand of (B.92) vanishes on the face of $\gamma$ unless $\gamma=\Gamma_1[S]$, the resistors of the induced subnetwork $\Gamma[S]$ on a set of nodes $S$, with
\Gamma[S]\ \text{connected},\qquad |\Gamma_1[S]|=2|S|-3,\qquad 2\le|S|\le|\Gamma_0|-1 .\tag{B.99}
Then $\Gamma/\gamma=\Gamma(S)$, the network with $\Gamma[S]$ shrunk to one node carrying $\sum_{v\in S}\lambda_v$ [15, Section 3.5], and $|\Gamma(S)_1|=2|\Gamma(S)_0|-3$.
Proof.
(a) Degree.
The two factors of (B.98) have degrees $2h_1(\gamma)$ and $2h_1(\Gamma/\gamma)$ along the two factors of (B.95), and

h_1(\gamma)+h_1(\Gamma/\gamma)=h_1(\Gamma_1),\qquad
2h_1(\Gamma_1)=|\Gamma_1|-2=\bigl(|\gamma|-1\bigr)+\bigl(|\Gamma_1\setminus\gamma|-1\bigr),
so a nonzero top form requires
2h_1(\gamma)=|\gamma|-1,\qquad 2h_1(\Gamma/\gamma)=|\Gamma_1\setminus\gamma|-1 .
(b) Separate islands.

If $\gamma$ has two or more islands $\gamma^{(1)},\gamma^{(2)},\ldots$, the island currents depend on $r_\gamma$ only through the ratios inside each island: the relative size of two islands shorted at a common rate moves no current (Figure 53(b)).
The first factor of (B.98) factors through a space of dimension $\sum_j(|\gamma^{(j)}|-1)\le|\gamma|-2$, below the degree $2h_1(\gamma)=|\gamma|-1$ required in (a), and vanishes.
(c) Bypassed resistor.
A resistor $f\notin\gamma$ with both terminals in the island is a self-loop of $\Gamma/\gamma$, hence a chord of every $T'$, and $y_f=0$ on the face by Lemma B.10(i) (Figure 53(a)), so $d^2y_f=0$.
(d) Laman island.
By (b) and (c), $\gamma=\Gamma_1[S]$ with $\Gamma[S]$ connected, $h_1(\gamma)=|\gamma|-|S|+1$, and
2h_1(\gamma)=|\gamma|-1\iff|\Gamma_1[S]|=2|S|-3
(Figure 53(c)).
$\gamma e\emptyset$ gives $|S|\ge2$; $\gamma e\Gamma_1$ gives $S e\Gamma_0$.
If two outer resistors join one node to two nodes of $S$, they are parallel in $\Gamma(S)$, and that face vanishes by [(3.11)](#eq-1-13).

Lemma B.13 (Factorization of a short).
Let $\gamma=\Gamma_1[S]$.

Each Taylor coefficient in $z$ of $\mathcal I^{\mathrm{raw\ cut}}_{\Gamma[S]}(\lambda^\gamma;z)$ is a polynomial in the island sources $\lambda^\gamma$, and the integral of (B.98) over $\mathbb{RP}^{|\Gamma_1[S]|-1}_{>0}\times\mathbb{RP}^{|\Gamma(S)_1|-1}_{>0}$ with the orientation $\eta_{\Gamma[S]}\wedge\eta_{\Gamma(S)}$ is
\mathcal I^{\mathrm{raw\ cut}}_{\Gamma[S]}(\lambda+\partial;z)\,\mathcal I^{\mathrm{raw\ cut}}_{\Gamma(S)}(\lambda;z),\tag{B.103}
the resistors of $\Gamma[S]$ and $\Gamma(S)$ ordered as in $\Gamma$ and the operators $(\lambda+\partial)_v$ acting on $\mathcal I^{\mathrm{raw\ cut}}_{\Gamma(S)}$.
By (B.102), (B.103) does not depend on how the island polynomial is extended off $\sum_{v\in S}\lambda^\gamma_v=0$.
Proof.

The island currents are linear in the island sources, so each Taylor coefficient of the first factor of (B.98) is a polynomial in $\lambda^\gamma$ times a form of top degree along $\mathbb{RP}^{|\Gamma_1[S]|-1}_{>0}$.
Integrating over the island ratios first,

\int(B.98)
=\int_{\mathbb{RP}^{|\Gamma(S)_1|-1}_{>0}}
\mathcal I^{\mathrm{raw\ cut}}_{\Gamma[S]}\bigl(\lambda^\gamma;z\bigr)\,
e^{-\sum_{e\notin\Gamma_1[S]}z_e^{+\dot a}y_{e,+\dot a}}\bigwedge_{c}\bigl(-d^2y_c\bigr),
and by (B.101) the sources $\lambda^\gamma$ are $(\lambda+\partial)$ acting on the exponential, outside the integral (Figure 54(b)).

blocks.source: Lemma B.14 (Orientation of a short).

For $\emptyset\ne\gamma\subsetneq\Gamma_1$ let $\pi_\gamma$ be the permutation of $\Gamma_1$ that moves the resistors of $\gamma$ to the front, keeping the relative order inside $\gamma$ and inside $\Gamma_1\setminus\gamma$.
With the outward normal first, the face (B.95) is oriented as a boundary face of $\bigl(\widehat{(0,+\infty)^{|\Gamma_1|}}/\mathbb R_+,\eta_\Gamma\bigr)$ by
(-1)^{|\gamma|+1}\mathop{\mathrm{sgn}}(\pi_\gamma)\,\eta_\gamma\wedge\eta_{\Gamma_1\setminus\gamma}.\tag{B.104}

For $\gamma=\Gamma_1[S]$ as in [(B.99)](#eq-sc-island), $|\gamma|=2|S|-3$ is odd and [(B.104)](#eq-sc-orient) is $\mathop{\mathrm{sgn}}(\pi_S)\,\eta_{\Gamma[S]}\wedge\eta_{\Gamma(S)}$, $\pi_S=\pi_{\Gamma_1[S]}$.
Proof.
In the collar coordinates $t_e=s\,r_e$ ($e\in\gamma$, $\sum_{e\in\gamma}r_e=1$) and $t_e=w_e$ ($e\notin\gamma$), $\bigwedge_{e\in\gamma}dr_e=0$, so
With $E=s\,\partial_s+\sum_{e\notin\gamma}w_e\partial/\partial w_e$ and $\iota_E\eta_\gamma=0$,
\eta_\Gamma=\mathop{\mathrm{sgn}}(\pi_\gamma)\,s^{|\gamma|-1}\Bigl[s\,\eta_\gamma\wedge\bigwedge_{e\notin\gamma}dw_e-(-1)^{|\gamma|-1}ds\wedge\eta_\gamma\wedge\eta_{\Gamma_1\setminus\gamma}\Bigr].
On the slice $\sum_{e\notin\gamma}w_e=1$ the first term vanishes:
\eta_\Gamma=(-1)^{|\gamma|+1}\mathop{\mathrm{sgn}}(\pi_\gamma)\,s^{|\gamma|-1}\,(-ds)\wedge\eta_\gamma\wedge\eta_{\Gamma_1\setminus\gamma}.
The interior is $s>0$ and the outward normal is $-\partial_s$.

For two resistors $(a,b)$ in series (Figure [55](#fig-sc-orient)(b)), $\eta_\Gamma=-ds$ on the slice $t_b=1$, with $s=t_a/t_b$: the short of $a$ ($s=0$) has orientation $+1$, the short of $b$ ($s=\infty$) has $-1=\mathop{\mathrm{sgn}}(\pi_{\{b\}})$.

blocks.source: Theorem B.15 (Short-circuit identity).
Let $\Gamma$ be a connected circuit without self-loops, with oriented resistors in a fixed order and $|\Gamma_1|=2|\Gamma_0|-4$.
For sources with $\sum_{v\in\Gamma_0}\lambda_v=0$ and formal displacements $z$,
summed over the $S\subseteq\Gamma_0$ of (B.99).

$\Gamma[S]$ and $\Gamma(S)$ keep the orientations and the relative order of their resistors in $\Gamma$, the merged node of $\Gamma(S)$ carries $\sum_{v\in S}\lambda_v$, $(\lambda+\partial)$ is (B.100) and $\pi_S$ is the shuffle of Lemma B.14.
Terms in which $\Gamma(S)$ has parallel resistors vanish.
Proof.
Let $\lambda$ be real.
The integrand of (B.92) extends to $\widehat{(0,+\infty)^{|\Gamma_1|}}/\mathbb R_+$.
By Lemma B.8, Stokes’ theorem on this compact manifold with corners (Figure 56), Proposition B.12, Lemma B.14 and Lemma B.13,
The face integrals carry the orientation $\eta_{\Gamma[S]}\wedge\eta_{\Gamma(S)}$; faces of codimension two and higher do not contribute.
Each Taylor coefficient in $z$ is a polynomial in $\lambda$, so (B.105) holds for all $\lambda$.

With the shuffle sign $\sigma(\Gamma',\Gamma/\Gamma')$ of [7, Section 4.1], which puts the outer resistors first, $(-1)^{\sigma(\Gamma[S],\Gamma/\Gamma[S])}=(-1)^{|\Gamma_1[S]|\,|\Gamma_1\setminus\Gamma_1[S]|}\mathop{\mathrm{sgn}}(\pi_S)=-\mathop{\mathrm{sgn}}(\pi_S)$ on every term of [(B.105)](#eq-sc-identity), both resistor counts being odd; [7, Equation (4.8)] at $d=2$ has the relative signs of [(B.105)](#eq-sc-identity).

blocks.source: Quadratic identities of the brackets.
For $k$ entries, (3.10) leaves circuits with $|\Gamma_1|=2k-3$ and $n=k-2$ loops.

Inserting (B.11) in (3.1), with the jet rule (A.34) turning holomorphic derivatives of contracted letters into $z_e$-derivatives of the kernel and (A.32) moving the letters left at node $v$ to the origin, with $\lambda_v=\partial/\partial x_v^+$ acting on them,
with $W_\Gamma[\mathcal O_1,\ldots,\mathcal O_k]=\Delta_{e_1}\Delta_{e_2}\cdots\Delta_{e_{|\Gamma_1|}}(\mathcal O_1\cdots\mathcal O_k)$ and $\Delta_e=\Delta_{e(0)e(1)}$ of (B.1), as in (A.33).
Each $\Delta_e$ pairs an even with an odd letter:
\Delta_e\Delta_{e'}=-\Delta_{e'}\Delta_e,\qquad\Delta_e^2=0;\tag{B.107}
$W_\Gamma$ and, through $\eta_\Gamma$, $\mathcal I^{\mathrm{raw\ cut}}_\Gamma$ both change sign under an odd reordering of the resistors, and their product does not.

Relabelling ungrounded nodes permutes the circuits $\Gamma$, so $(-1)^{\sum_i(k-i)|\mathcal O_i|}\{\mathcal O_1,\ldots,\mathcal O_k\}_0$ depends on $\mathcal O_1,\ldots,\mathcal O_{k-1}$ only through the graded-commutative product $\mathcal O_1\cdots\mathcal O_k$:
By [(B.13)](#eq-1-2) and [(A.34)](#eq-W-jet-edge), on a letter of $\mathcal O_v$ that a resistor $e$ carries away,
Let $\Gamma$ be almost Laman on $k$ nodes, $S=\{i_1<\cdots(B.99), $S^c=\{j_1<\cdots57).
An outer resistor at $\ast$ contracts a letter of the island bracket, that is, a letter of some $\mathcal O_v$, $v\in S$:
\Delta_{\ast u}=\sum_{v\in S}\Delta_{vu}.\tag{B.110}

By (B.109) the island momentum $\lambda_v$ on the letters carried away by outer resistors becomes the $z$-derivatives of (B.100): the island is fed at $v$ by $(\lambda+\partial)_v$, its source plus the currents of the outer resistors at $v$ (Figure 49(b)).
The outer source $\lambda_\ast=\sum_{v\in S}\lambda_v$ acts on the letters left in the output.

The island bracket grounds the island at $i_{|S|}$: it replaces the island source $(\lambda+\partial)_{i_{|S|}}$ by $-\sum_{v\in S\setminus i_{|S|}}(\lambda+\partial)_v$, and the difference annihilates $\mathcal I^{\mathrm{raw\ cut}}_{\Gamma(S)}$ by (B.102), so the island may be grounded at any of its nodes.
The node $k$ of $\Gamma$ stays grounded: for $k\in S$ the island bracket occupies the grounded slot.
In both cases it is placed in the slot of its last entry,

P^{(S)}=\bigl(\mathcal O_{j_1},\ldots,\mathcal O_{j_p},\ \{\mathcal O_{i_1},\ldots,\mathcal O_{i_{|S|}}\}_0,\ \mathcal O_{j_{p+1}},\ldots,\mathcal O_{j_{k-|S|}}\bigr),\qquad j_p<i_{|S|}<j_{p+1}.\tag{B.111}
By [(B.110)](#eq-sc-star) the outer contractions act after the island contractions; with [(B.107)](#eq-sc-odd),
$W_{\Gamma[S]}$, $W_{\Gamma(S)}$ the ordered products of the $\Delta_e$ of $W_\Gamma$ over the island and over the outer resistors.
The orientation sign of the short is the reordering sign of the contractions; the remaining $-1$ is common to all $S$.
Multiplying (B.105) by $W_\Gamma$,

\sum_S\mathcal I^{\mathrm{raw\ cut}}_{\Gamma[S]}(\lambda+\partial;z)\,\mathcal I^{\mathrm{raw\ cut}}_{\Gamma(S)}(\lambda;z)\,
W_{\Gamma(S)}W_{\Gamma[S]}(\mathcal O_1\cdots\mathcal O_k)=0 .\tag{B.113}
The terms pair as
\bigl(\Gamma',\ \Gamma'',\ \text{a node of }S\text{ for each outer resistor at }\ast\bigr)\ \longleftrightarrow\ (\Gamma,S),\qquad \Gamma[S]=\Gamma',\quad\Gamma(S)=\Gamma'' .

A resistor of $\Gamma$ between two nodes of $S$ outside $\Gamma'$ would be a shorted resistor at $\ast$, so $\Gamma'$ is the induced subnetwork; two outer resistors from different nodes of $S$ to one node $u$ are parallel in $\Gamma''$, with kernel zero by (3.11) and $\Delta_{\ast u}^2=0$.
The normalizations combine to $(-8\pi^2)^{-(|S|-2)-(k-|S|-1)}=(-8\pi^2)^{3-k}$ for every $S$.

For $k\ge3$ homogeneous entries,

blocks.source: Proof.
Stokes.
A marked almost-Laman circuit has one resistance ratio more than the real components of its loop currents, and its current form is closed (Lemma B.8).
Its integral over the boundary of the compactified ratio space vanishes.
The boundary consists of shorts, and a short contributes only when its island $S$ is a Laman network, which the outer network $\Gamma(S)$ sees as a single node (Proposition B.12, Theorem B.15).
Where the marked resistor goes.
A short closes every resistor between two nodes of its island.
If $A,B\in S$, the marked resistor is shorted with the island, and the auxiliary pair is contracted inside it.
If $A\in S$ and $B\notin S$, no resistor of the island reaches $B$: the letter $a$ rides to the merged node uncontracted, and the marked resistor joins the merged node to $B$ in the outer network.
The same holds with $A$ and $B$ exchanged.
If $A,B\notin S$, the marked resistor joins $A$ to $B$ outside the island.
What the merged node carries.
By Lemma B.13 and (B.111), the island fed by the outer network is the island bracket placed at the merged node.
(i) $A,B\in S$: the island is a marked graph of $\{\mathcal I^{\otimes r},A,B\}^{\gamma,0}$, $r!$ times the coefficient of $\hbar^r$ in $A\star B$.
The outer network has $N-r$ interaction nodes, the merged node and $2(N-r+1)-3$ resistors: a graph of $Q_{N-r-1}$ acting on it.

(ii) $A\in S$, $B\notin S$: the island is a graph of $\{\mathcal I^{\otimes r},A\}_0=r!\,Q_{r-1}A$, with $a$ riding along, and the outer network, a marked graph with $N-r$ interaction nodes, multiplies it with $B$.
(iii) $B\in S$, $A\notin S$: as in (ii), with $A$ and $B$ exchanged.
(iv) $A,B\notin S$: the merged node carries $\{\mathcal I^{\otimes r}\}_0$, $r\ge2$, into a marked graph.
Weights and signs.

Distributing the $N$ interaction nodes between the island and the outer network gives $\binom Nr$ equal terms, and $\binom Nr/N!=1/(r!\,(N-r)!)$ splits $\hbar^{N-1}/N!$ into the weights of $\mathbf Q$ in (5.3) and of $\star$ in (5.4); in (iv), into the weight $\hbar^{r-2}/r!$ of (7.9) and $\hbar^{N-r+1}/(N-r)!$ of the outer marked graph, as in (5.8).

C Heat-kernel transfer and the quantum differential
We review the BV construction of the holomorphically twisted theory in Costello’s formalism [5], using the ultraviolet finiteness of holomorphic graph integrals proved in [7; 23].
Starting from the BV Ward identity for an insertion, we rederive the loop corrections $Q_n$ of [16; 15] to its local transformation and recover the graph formula (7.1) of Section 7.

The normalized finite-scale expression (C.9) is evaluated at fixed $L$ before passing to the projective kernel.
Finally, the QME makes the scale-$L$ BV differential square to zero.
Applying (C.14) twice and using (C.11) gives

\mathbf Q^2=0,\qquad
\sum_{r=0}^{n}Q_rQ_{n-r}=0\quad(n\ge0).\tag{C.20}

These are also the quadratic identities of the local higher operations [8, Section 3], [15, Equations (3.21) and (4.17)] (Stokes proof in [7, Theorem 7]), applied to the interacting brackets [15, Equations (4.44)–(4.45)].
D Feynman rules of the twisted theory
This appendix collects, with their coefficients and signs, the rules from which every graph of the article is evaluated.
The rules are those of the body, cited where they enter; the statements on coordinates, orientations and orderings make explicit the conventions these rules use.
Appendix D.7 evaluates examples with them.
D.1 Coordinates, gradings and the Lie algebra
The coordinates and forms are those of [(A.1)](#eq-Euclidean-coordinates), [(A.2)](#eq-coordinates) and the volume relation after [(A.12)](#eq-B-7):

\begin{gathered}
x^{a\dot a}=x_E^\mu\sigma_\mu^{a\dot a},\qquad
\frac{\partial}{\partial x^{a\dot a}}=-\frac12\partial_{a\dot a},\qquad
\epsilon^{\dot+\dot-}=1=-\epsilon_{\dot+\dot-},\qquad
\epsilon^{+-}=1=-\epsilon_{+-},\\
dx^-_{\dot a}=\epsilon_{\dot a\dot b}dx^{-\dot b},\qquad
\bar\partial=dx^{-\dot a}\frac{\partial}{\partial x^{-\dot a}},\qquad
\Omega=2\,dx^{+\dot+}\wedge dx^{+\dot-},\qquad
\Omega\wedge dx^{-\dot+}\wedge dx^{-\dot-}=-8\,d^4x_E,\\
w_+{}^{\dot a}=\epsilon^{\dot a\dot b}w_{+\dot b},\qquad
u_{+\dot a}w_+{}^{\dot a}=u_{+\dot+}w_{+\dot-}-u_{+\dot-}w_{+\dot+},\qquad
|x|_E^2=x^{+\dot c}\epsilon_{\dot c\dot d}x^{-\dot d},
\end{gathered}\tag{D.1}
with $d^4x_E=dx_E^0\wedge dx_E^1\wedge dx_E^2\wedge dx_E^3$.

The last identity equates the exponents of (B.3) and (B.14) at $z_e=0$; at real points $x^{-\dot a}$ is $\epsilon^{\dot a\dot b}$ times the complex conjugate of $x^{+\dot b}$, so that $|x|_E^2=\sum_{\dot a}|x^{+\dot a}|^2$.
