D.4 Graphs, signs and normalization

For homogeneous operators $\mathcal O_1,\ldots,\mathcal O_k$ with $\mathcal O_k$ at the origin, the bracket $\{\mathcal O_1,\ldots,\mathcal O_k\}_0$ of [(3.1)](#eq-A-28) is evaluated by the following rules.
(R1) Graphs.
Sum over connected labelled graphs $\Gamma$ on the vertices $1,\ldots,k$, the vertex $v$ carrying $\mathcal O_v(x_v)$.
The vertices are distinguishable: graphs that differ by a relabelling of interaction vertices are distinct terms, and no factor $1/|\mathrm{Aut}\,\Gamma|$ occurs.

Each edge contracts a $\mathsf c$ with a $\mathsf b$ or a $\gamma$ with a $\beta$ at two different vertices, $\Delta_{vw}$ summing over the pairs of letters it can contract; contractions inside one input are excluded.
(R2) Order and orientation.
Order the edges $e_1,\ldots,e_{|\Gamma_1|}$ and orient them, $e_a=(v_a,w_a)$.
(R3) Spacetime factor.

For $j=1,\ldots,|\Gamma_1|$, the edge $e_j$ carries $[K_{\varepsilon;e_j}]_\Omega$ and every other edge $[P_{\varepsilon,L;e_a}]_\Omega$, wedged in edge order, with the sign $(-1)^{j-1}$; the $j$-sum is the action of $\bar\partial$ on the ordered propagators (C.12), restricted to its lower boundaries.
(R4) Fibre factor.

The ordered contraction (A.33) applies $\Delta_{v_1w_1}\Delta_{v_2w_2}\cdots\Delta_{v_{|\Gamma_1|}w_{|\Gamma_1|}}$ to the ordered product $\mathcal O_1\cdots\mathcal O_k$, the operators acting from right to left: $\Delta_{v_{|\Gamma_1|}w_{|\Gamma_1|}}$ first, and in each term of $\Delta_{vw}$ the right-hand derivative first.

A left derivative $\partial_L/\partial X$ acquires $(-1)^{|X||Y|}$ for every letter $Y$ it passes, $|X|,|Y|$ the fermion numbers of Table 6: $\partial_L/\partial\mathsf c$ and $\partial_L/\partial\beta$ acquire $-1$ for every odd letter, $\partial_L/\partial\mathsf b$ and $\partial_L/\partial\gamma$ no sign.
A contracted letter carrying holomorphic derivatives is removed by (A.34).
(R5) Output and integration.

Project each surviving letter with $\pi$ of (A.31) to its holomorphic zero-form jet, $X(x_v)\mapsto\exp(x_v^{+\dot a}\partial/\partial x^{+\dot a})X^{(0)}(0)$ (C.8); integrate $\int_{(\mathbb C^2)^{k-1}}\bigwedge_{v0$.
(R6) Global sign.
Multiply by $(-1)^{\sum_{i=1}^k(k-i)|\mathcal O_i|}$; it is $+1$ when every entry but the last is even.

Changing the edge order changes the spacetime factor and $\prod_a\Delta_{v_aw_a}$ by the same sign: propagators are one-forms and $\Delta_{vw}$ is odd, while moving the heat edge, a two-form, also changes $(-1)^{j-1}$.

blocks.source: E Algorithm for the lifting tests

This appendix gives the algorithm behind the lifting tests of Section [9](#sec-applications) and reports what it finds when the finite-dimensional computation of Section [8.3](#sec-homotopy-transfer) is run over every charge sector of a theory up to a fixed level.

In each sector the computation returns the dimension $h$ of the classical cohomology $E_1=H(Q_0)$, the rank $\rho$ of its restriction to Cartan-valued letters, the number $f$ of fortuitous classes, which do not come from the cohomology at large rank, and the ranks of the successive differentials $d_r$ of [(8.29)](#eq-page-differentials).

Appendix [E.1](#sec-E-alg) sets up the grading that makes each sector finite, the reduction to highest-weight cochains, their evaluation at finite rank, the rank formulas that the programs evaluate, the comparison with the stable cohomology, and the certification of the ranks.

Appendix [E.2](#sec-E-SU) lists the fortuitous classes found in $\mathcal N=4$ Yang–Mills theory with gauge group $SU(N)$ and shows that each class tested survives at every perturbative order, or at least through the orders computed.

Appendix [E.3](#sec-E-SOSp) finds the first fortuitous classes of $SO(2N+1)$ and $Sp(N)$ and shows that the one-loop differential removes every classical difference between the two S-dual theories, charge by charge, at all levels computed.

Appendix [E.4](#sec-E-gram) proves two theorems on commuting schemes that explain the non-Cartan classes behind these differences: the Gram determinant spans the $SL_d$-invariant part of degree $2d$ of the invariant ring for $d<h^\vee$ and is a nonzero nilpotent with zero Cartan restriction for $\operatorname{rk}\mathfrak g<d<h^\vee$, contradicting a conjecture of Chen and Ngô, and a lemma used by Song, Xia and Xu fails for every $d\ge2$.
Appendix [E.5](#sec-E-G2) applies the first theorem to $G_2$, where it gives a purely scalar class that survives at every order, and reports the census of $G_2$ theory.

Appendix [E.6](#sec-E-LS) shows that in the Leigh–Strassler deformation of $SU(3)$ theory the two-loop differential is nonzero at many levels; its sources form translation towers, its rank is fixed by $Q_0$, $Q_1$ and nilpotence, and at the lowest hits it vanishes exactly where the theory is equivalent to a $\beta$-deformation, while the $\beta$-deformation has its own first two-loop lift at a higher level.
Appendix [E.7](#sec-E-N2) shows that $\mathcal N=2$ quiver and SQCD theories and their mass deformations have $d_2=d_3=0$ on every candidate pair.
The tables of all computed sectors are collected in the repository lbotao399-stack/quantum-lifts-results.
E.1 The census algorithm
The census applies the page-by-page computation of Section [8.3](#sec-homotopy-transfer) to every sector of a level.

Its steps are the grading of Appendix [E.1.1](#sec-E-sectors), the highest-weight cochains of Appendix [E.1.2](#sec-E-hw) and their evaluation in Appendix [E.1.3](#sec-E-eval), the ranks of Appendix [E.1.4](#sec-E-pages), the restrictions of Appendix [E.1.5](#sec-E-fort), the selection rules of Appendix [E.1.6](#sec-E-select) and the certification of Appendix [E.1.7](#sec-E-cert); Appendix [E.1.8](#sec-E-chain) follows one class through all of them.
E.1.1 Charge sectors and the grading of the loop corrections
A sector must be specified by quantities that every $Q_n$ shifts by a fixed amount; then each sector is finite-dimensional and each $d_r$ connects two definite sectors.

The letters $\gamma^I,\beta_I,\mathsf b$ and $\partial_{+\dot a}\mathsf c$ of Section [8.1](#sec-graviton-closure), with their holomorphic derivatives, carry three flavour weights, the numbers of $\theta_I$ indices they occupy in the superfield as in Section [9.2](#sec-finite-sectors), and the two derivative totals $n_\pm$ of Section [8.3](#sec-homotopy-transfer), the numbers of $\partial_{+\dot+}$ and $\partial_{+\dot-}$.
For a monomial with $Y$ letters we write

\begin{gathered}\lambda=(\theta_1,\theta_2,\theta_3;n_+,n_-),\qquad \Theta=\theta_1+\theta_2+\theta_3,\qquad \mathsf d=(1,1,1;-1,-1),\\ \theta(\gamma^I)=e_I,\qquad \theta(\beta_I)=(1,1,1)-e_I,\qquad \theta(\mathsf b)=(1,1,1),\qquad \theta(\mathsf c)=0,\end{gathered}\tag{E.1}
where $e_I$ is the $I$th unit vector; $\Theta$ is the component degree $\deg_\theta$ of [(8.9)](#eq-2-62).
The cochains of weight $\lambda$ with $Y$ letters form the sector $C^Y(\lambda)$, and we write $(\lambda)_Y$ for it.
The corresponding operator of the untwisted theory has scaling dimension $E$, $SU(4)_R$ Cartan charges $R_I$ in the basis that rotates the three adjoint chiral multiplets, and spins $J_L,J_R$:

\begin{gathered}E=\tfrac12(\Theta+Y)+n_++n_-,\qquad R_I=\theta_I-\tfrac12(\Theta-Y),\\ J_L=\tfrac12(\Theta-Y+n_++n_-),\qquad J_R=\tfrac12(n_+-n_-),\\ E=R_1+R_2+R_3+2J_L,\qquad 2(E+J_L)=2\Theta+3(n_++n_-).\end{gathered}\tag{E.2}
The letters carry the charges

$\gamma^I$scalar $\bar\phi_I$$e_I$$(0,0)$$1$$e_I$$0$$0$
$\beta_I$fermion $\psi^I_+$$(1,1,1)-e_I$$(0,0)$$\tfrac32$$(\tfrac12,\tfrac12,\tfrac12)-e_I$$\tfrac12$$0$

Every cochain saturates the bound $E=R_1+R_2+R_3+2J_L$ of the $1/16$-BPS states.
We call $E+J_L$ the level; by the last relation in [(E.2)](#eq-E-charges), a level contains finitely many sectors.

For example, the threshold class [(9.25)](#eq-threshold-source) of $SU(2)$ has two $\gamma$, five $\beta$ and no derivatives, so $\lambda=(4,4,4;0,0)$, $Y=7$, and [(E.2)](#eq-E-charges) gives $E=\tfrac{19}2$, $R_I=\tfrac32$, $J_L=\tfrac52$ and level $E+J_L=12$.
Proposition E.1.
*For every $n\ge0$ and every $r\ge1$,*
Q_n:C^Y(\lambda)\to C^{Y+1-n}(\lambda-n\mathsf d),\qquad d_r:E_r^Y(\lambda)\to E_r^{Y+1-r}(\lambda-r\mathsf d).\tag{E.3}
*Both maps change the charges [(E.2)](#eq-E-charges) by $(\Delta E;\Delta R_I;\Delta J_L,\Delta J_R)=(\tfrac12;\tfrac12,\tfrac12,\tfrac12;-\tfrac12,0)$, independently of $n$ and $r$.*
*Proof.* The fan of $Q_n$ in [(7.3)](#eq-2-8) has $n+1$ interaction vertices and $2n+1$ contractions: one spoke to each of the $n+1$ contracted letters of the operator and $n$ edges along the chain.
The vertices have $3(n+1)$ legs, the contractions use $(n+1)+2n$ of them, and the two remaining legs are the output superfields, so $Y$ changes by $-(n+1)+2=1-n$.

Each vertex carries $\int d^3\theta$, which supplies one unit of every $\theta_I$, and each contraction pairs components whose flavour weights add to $(1,1,1)$, since $\theta(\gamma^I)+\theta(\beta_I)=\theta(\mathsf c)+\theta(\mathsf b)=(1,1,1)$; the flavour weight therefore changes by $(n+1)(1,1,1)-(2n+1)(1,1,1)=-n(1,1,1)$, which refines [(8.11)](#eq-graviton-differential-degree).
By [(8.48)](#eq-derivative-homogeneity), $Q_n$ adds $n$ derivatives in each holomorphic direction.

Every term of $d_r$ in [(8.25)](#eq-page-transfer) is a composition $Q_{k_1}hQ_{k_2}h\cdots hQ_{k_m}$ with $k_1+\cdots+k_m=r$ and homogeneous homotopies $h$ of degree $Y\mapsto Y-1$; its total shift is $\sum_i(1-k_i)-(m-1)=1-r$ letters and $-r\mathsf d$ in weight.
Substituting $\Delta\lambda=-n\mathsf d$, $\Delta Y=1-n$ in [(E.2)](#eq-E-charges) gives $\Delta\Theta=-3n$, $\Delta(n_++n_-)=2n$ and the stated charges.

The loop order of a pairing is thus invisible in the physical charges and recorded only by the cochain grading: the sectors $(\lambda+k\mathsf d)_{Y+k}$, $k\in\mathbb Z$, carry the same charges, and $d_r$ joins a source to the member with $k=r-1$ of the target family.
Nonnegativity of the weights gives two selection rules.
Corollary E.2.
*An outgoing differential $d_r$ from $(\lambda)_Y$ is possible only if $\theta_I\ge r$ for $I=1,2,3$. An incoming $d_r$ into $(\lambda)_Y$ is possible only if $n_\pm\ge r$.*
*Proof.* The target of an outgoing $d_r$ has flavour weights $\theta_I-r\ge0$, and the source of an incoming one has derivative totals $n_\pm-r\ge0$; the second statement is Lemma [8.2](#b-00758).
E.1.2 Highest-weight cochains

The flavour rotations of the $\theta_I$ and the rotations of the dotted index act on the letters, and their raising operators $E_{12}$, $E_{23}$ and $J_+$ commute with every $Q_n$: the interaction in [(7.3)](#eq-2-8) is $SL(3)$-invariant, the kernel depends on the odd coordinates only through the differences [(8.5)](#eq-graviton-odd-factor), and the dotted indices are contracted with $\epsilon^{\dot a\dot b}$.
Each $Q_n$ and each $d_r$ therefore maps highest-weight cochains to highest-weight cochains, and every rank is determined by its values on
\begin{gathered}C^Y_{\mathrm{HW}}(\lambda)=C^Y(\lambda)\cap\ker E_{12}\cap\ker E_{23}\cap\ker J_+,\\ \theta_1\ge\theta_2\ge\theta_3\ge0,\qquad n_+\ge n_-\ge0.\end{gathered}\tag{E.4}
A highest-weight class of $(\lambda)_Y$ stands for a full multiplet of $SU(3)\times SU(2)$; the number of states it represents is the product of the dimensions of the two irreducible representations.

On a letter carrying $r$ derivatives $\partial_{+\dot+}$ and $s$ derivatives $\partial_{+\dot-}$, record the jet by the monomial $u^rv^s$; then $J_+=u\,\partial_v$, and a letter type together with its order $r+s$ is a skeleton entry.

The space [(E.4)](#eq-E-hw) splits into blocks labelled by the multiset of skeleton entries, and its dimension in each block is the colour-singlet multiplicity, computed exactly by Weyl integration of the character of the letters over the gauge group, alternated over the Weyl groups of $SU(3)$ and $SU(2)$.
For $SU(2)$ and $SU(3)$ the highest-weight cochains are produced by contracting three tableaux.

In the flavour tableau each $\gamma^I$ carries a vector index, each $\beta_I$ the wedge $e_{I+1}\wedge e_{I+2}$, $\mathsf b$ the top wedge $e_1\wedge e_2\wedge e_3$ and $\mathsf c$ nothing, so that a column of wedges is a highest-weight vector of $GL(3)$.
The dotted tableau consists of $n_-$ brackets $[pq]=u_pv_q-v_pu_q$ of the jet variables of two letters and $n_+-n_-$ further factors $u$.
The colour part is a trace word of the matrix letters.
The resulting spanning set is checked against the exact dimension in each block, and for $SU(3)$ it is split by charge conjugation $C:t_A\mapsto-t_A^{\mathsf T}$ into its even and odd parts.

For $SU(N)$ with $N\ge4$ the letters and their derivatives are organized by the super vector space $V=\mathbb C^{3|2}$ spanned by $\theta_1,\theta_2,\theta_3$ and the two holomorphic coordinates, and the cochains decompose into highest weights of $\mathfrak{gl}(3|2)$ labelled by Young diagrams $\mu$ with $\mu_4\le2$.
A diagram with $|\mu|=\Theta+n_++n_-$ boxes corresponds to the sector weight and level
\begin{gathered}\lambda(\mu)=\bigl(\mu_1,\mu_2,\mu_3;\ \#\{i\ge4:\mu_i\ge1\},\ \#\{i\ge4:\mu_i\ge2\}\bigr),\\ 2(E+J_L)=2(\mu_1+\mu_2+\mu_3)+3\sum_{i\ge4}\mu_i,\end{gathered}\tag{E.5}
in agreement with [(E.2)](#eq-E-charges), since $\mu_i\le2$ for $i\ge4$.
Each level then involves only a few diagrams.
E.1.3 Evaluation at finite rank

The cochains are realized by spanning sets of trace words, or of invariant tensors for $SO$, $Sp$ and $G_2$, evaluated at random Lie-algebra-valued letters modulo the prime $p=2^{31}-1$; a cochain is represented by its vector of values.
The trace identities of the chosen rank then hold automatically, and agreement of the rank of the spanning set with the exact dimension certifies that it spans the sector.

For $SU(N)$ the letters are traceless $N\times N$ matrices with random entries, the last diagonal entry fixed by tracelessness, and the Casimir tensor of the fundamental representation is $\sum_R(t_R)_{ab}(t^R)_{cd}=\delta_{ad}\delta_{bc}-\tfrac1N\delta_{ab}\delta_{cd}$ with $t^R=\kappa^{RS}t_S$ and $\kappa_{RS}=\operatorname{tr}(t_Rt_S)$.

For $SO(2n+1)$ and $Sp(n)$ the letters satisfy $A^{\mathsf T}F+FA=0$ with $F_{i\bar\imath}=1$, respectively $F_{i\bar\imath}=s_i$ with $s_i=+1$ for $i\le n$ and $-1$ otherwise, where $\bar\imath=N_F+1-i$ and $N_F=2n+1$ or $2n$; then
\sum_R(t_R)_{ab}(t^R)_{cd}=\tfrac12\delta_{ad}\delta_{bc}-\tfrac12F_{ac}F_{bd}.\tag{E.6}

On a word, $Q_n$ of [(7.3)](#eq-2-8) removes $n+1$ letters, replaces them by the two derivative-carrying output letters joined by the chain of structure constants $C_{A_1DR_1}C_{A_2R_1R_2}\cdots C_{A_{n+1}R_nE}$, and multiplies by the coefficient of the Taylor term selected by the derivatives.
In a matrix realization the chain is a nested sequence of commutators,

Q_nF\ \ni\ F\bigl(\ldots,\underbrace{[P,t_{R_1}]}_{\text{slot }i_1},\ldots,\underbrace{[t^{R_1},t_{R_2}]}_{\text{slot }i_2},\ldots,\underbrace{[t^{R_n},Q]}_{\text{slot }i_{n+1}},\ldots\bigr),\tag{E.7}
summed over the ordered choices of the $n+1$ slots, where $P$ and $Q$ are the two output letters and the Casimir contractions [(E.6)](#eq-E-casimir) carry out the sums over $R_j$.
E.1.4 Ranks of the successive differentials
For the source sector $(\lambda)_Y$ let $\mathcal K$ be a basis of its $Q_0$-cocycles.
The first corrections, second corrections and so on lie in $C_m=C^{Y-m}(\lambda-m\mathsf d)$, and the order-$k$ residual lies in $C'_k=C^{Y+1-k}(\lambda-k\mathsf d)$.
Collect the source columns and the correction columns into the block lower-triangular matrices

\begin{gathered}M_R=\Bigl[\ \underbrace{Q_k\mathcal K}_{\text{source cocycles}}\ \Big|\ \underbrace{Q_{k-m}:C_m\to C'_k}_{\text{corrections}}\ \Bigr]_{1\le m\le k\le R},\qquad M'_R=M_R\setminus\{Q_k\mathcal K\},\\ \operatorname{rank}d_R=\bigl(\operatorname{rank}M_R-\operatorname{rank}M_{R-1}\bigr)-\bigl(\operatorname{rank}M'_R-\operatorname{rank}M'_{R-1}\bigr),\end{gathered}\tag{E.8}
with block row $k$ in $C'_k$ and $M_0=M'_0=0$.
Proposition E.3.
*Formula [(E.8)](#eq-E-rank) gives the rank of $d_R$ on $E_R^Y(\lambda)$. For $R=2$ it is the quotient test [(8.45)](#eq-d2-quotient-test).*
*Proof.* For a block lower-triangular matrix $\begin{pmatrix}A&0\\B&C\end{pmatrix}$, the rank equals $\operatorname{rank}A+\operatorname{rank}\bigl[B|_{\ker A}\ \ C\bigr]$.

Applied to $M'_2$, the difference $\operatorname{rank}M'_2-\operatorname{rank}M'_1$ is the dimension of $\operatorname{im}Q_0+Q_1\ker Q_0$ in $C'_2$, with $\ker Q_0$ in the first-correction sector $C_1$.

Applied to $M_2$, the difference $\operatorname{rank}M_2-\operatorname{rank}M_1$ is the dimension of the span of $\operatorname{im}Q_0+Q_1\ker Q_0$ together with the residuals $Q_2\mathcal O_0+Q_1\mathcal O_1$ of all pairs with $Q_1\mathcal O_0+Q_0\mathcal O_1=0$.
Their difference is the number of residuals independent modulo $\operatorname{im}Q_0+Q_1\ker Q_0$, which is [(8.45)](#eq-d2-quotient-test).

A classically exact source $\mathcal O_0=Q_0x$ has $\mathcal O_1=Q_1x+z$ with $Q_0z=0$, and $Q_1^2=-(Q_0Q_2+Q_2Q_0)$ gives the residual $-Q_0Q_2x+Q_1z$ inside the quotient; a $d_1$-exact source $\mathcal O_0=Q_1y$ with $Q_0y=0$ has $\mathcal O_1=Q_2y+z$ and residual $-Q_0Q_3y+Q_1z$ by the cubic nilpotence relation. Exact sources therefore contribute nothing, and the count is the rank of $d_2$ on $E_2$.
For general $R$ the same block identity applied to rows $1,\dots,R$ reproduces [(8.35)](#eq-2-75).

In practice the rows of each block are evaluated at random probe points and the columns are reduced modulo $p$; for the largest sectors a random linear projection of the rows selects the pivot columns, as in the pivot splitting of Section [8.3](#sec-homotopy-transfer).

When a single class is followed through several orders, the corrections $\mathcal O_r$ are obtained by solving $Q_0\mathcal O_r=-R_r$ with $R_r=\sum_{k=1}^rQ_k\mathcal O_{r-k}$, and $R_r\in\operatorname{im}Q_0$ is checked directly.
E.1.5 Cartan restriction and fortuity
The restriction of letters to a Cartan subalgebra $\mathfrak h$ sets the commutators in $Q_0$ to zero, so classical boundaries restrict to zero, as in Section [9.2](#sec-finite-sectors).
The restriction therefore induces a map on $E_1$, whose rank on $(\lambda)_Y$ we call $\rho$.
Classes in its kernel are the non-Cartan classes of [29, Definition 1].
A fortuitous class is a class of the rank-$N$ theory that does not come from the stable cohomology [20; 29, Definition 3].

Let $C_\infty$ be the cochain complex of the stable trace algebra, at rank large compared with the number of letters, and $\pi_N:C_\infty\to C_N$ the restriction to rank $N$, with kernel $R_N$ given by the trace identities.
With $B_N=\operatorname{im}Q_0$ at rank $N$,
f=h-\operatorname{rank}\pi_N^*,\qquad \operatorname{rank}\pi_N^*=\operatorname{rank}\begin{pmatrix}\pi_N&B_N\\ Q_0^\infty&0\end{pmatrix}-\operatorname{rank}Q_0^\infty-\operatorname{rank}B_N,\tag{E.9}
which is the block identity of Proposition E.3 applied to the columns of $C_\infty$ and of the boundaries $B_N$.

Since $\pi_N$ is surjective on cochains, the long exact sequence of $0\to R_N\to C_\infty\to C_N\to0$ identifies the fortuitous classes of degree $Y-1$ with the kernel $K(Y)$ of $H^Y(R_N)\to H^Y(C_\infty)$:

\begin{gathered}f(Y-1)=K(Y)=\dim R^Y-\operatorname{rank}\begin{pmatrix}Q:R^Y\to R^{Y+1}&0\\ \iota:R^Y\to C^Y_\infty&Q_0:C^{Y-1}_\infty\to C^Y_\infty\end{pmatrix}\\ +\operatorname{rank}Q_0\big|_{C^{Y-1}_\infty}-\operatorname{rank}Q\big|_{R^{Y-1}}.\end{gathered}\tag{E.10}

Indeed, the pairs $(z,w)\in R^Y\oplus C^{Y-1}_\infty$ with $Qz=0$ and $\iota z=Q_0w$ form the kernel of the block matrix, each admissible $z$ appears with $w$ fixed up to $\ker Q_0$, and the boundaries of $R$ are subtracted at the end.
For $SU(N)$ with $N\ge4$ the relation complex $R_N$ is computed diagram by diagram in the decomposition [(E.5)](#eq-E-young).
For $SU(N)$ the trace identities start at $N+1$ letters, so $SU(N)$ with $N\ge Y+1$ computes the stable cohomology of a sector with $Y$ letters.

For $SO(2n+1)$ and $Sp(n)$ the stable trace algebras of the orthogonal and symplectic series coincide, by the reversal identity of their trace words, and their counts are obtained by a Burnside sum over $\prod_kS_2\wr S_k$ acting on perfect matchings; sectors with fewer than $2n+2$, respectively $n+1$, letters lie in the stable range and have $f=0$.
E.1.6 Selection rules and the all-order criterion

By Theorem [8.1](#b-00630) and [(8.39)](#eq-graviton-dr-zero), every $d_r$ vanishes on the graviton part, so in each sector the ranks of all $d_r$ add up to at most the number of fortuitous classes of the source and of the target.

A class at $(\lambda)_Y$ survives at every perturbative order when each outgoing $d_r$ with $r\le\min_I\theta_I$ vanishes on it, which includes the case of a target with $E_r=0$, and each incoming $d_r$ with $r\le\min(n_+,n_-)$ misses it.
Both lists are finite by Corollary E.2, and a closed completion then exists order by order by [(8.35)](#eq-2-75).

For $SO(2N+1)$, $Sp(N)$, $G_2$, the Leigh–Strassler theory and the $\mathcal N=2$ theories the scans compute $h$ and $\rho$ in every sector of a level, $d_1$ on every pair with nonzero $E_1$ at both ends, and $d_2$, $d_3$ on every candidate pair with nonzero $E_r$ at both ends; for $SU(N)$ they compute $h$ and $f$ in every sector and the differentials on the fortuitous classes found.
E.1.7 Certification and gates
Unless stated otherwise, ranks are computed modulo $p=2^{31}-1$ at random probe points.

Such a rank is a lower bound for the rank over $\mathbb Q$ of the same matrix and equals it except on a set of probes and primes of small measure; it is exact when it equals the dimension of the source or of the target.

Entries marked [p,p′] are confirmed at the second prime $p'=2147483629$ with independent probes, and entries marked [$\mathbb Q$] are exact over $\mathbb Q$, either by elimination over $\mathbb Z$ or by the Chinese remainder theorem over enough primes to exceed the Hadamard bound of the minors.
Each program is gated before production runs.

The nilpotence relations $\sum_{j=0}^nQ_jQ_{n-j}=0$ for $n\le3$ are checked on random cochains of several sectors; altering one coefficient of $Q_2$ or $Q_3$, the sign of a vertex or a projection makes them fail.

Each new realization of a gauge group reproduces the known counts of a smaller one, for instance $SO(3)=Sp(1)$ and $SU(2)$, and $SO(5)=Sp(2)$, and the orbit sums used for $SO$, $Sp$ and large $SU(N)$ reproduce the full torus sums sector by sector.

E.4 Commuting schemes and non-Cartan classes

In the purely scalar sectors $n_\pm=0$, $Y=\Theta$, the top-degree classical cohomology is the space of invariant functions of the commuting triples $(\gamma^1,\gamma^2,\gamma^3)$, and its Cartan restriction is the restriction of such functions to $\mathfrak h^3$; more generally, the top-degree part of every sector is described by the super-commuting scheme of Chang [29, Proposition 4] in the super vector space spanned by $\theta_1,\theta_2,\theta_3$ and the two holomorphic coordinates.
This appendix determines one isotypic component of these invariant rings exactly.

It proves that the Gram determinant is a nonzero nilpotent invariant with zero Cartan restriction whenever $\operatorname{rk}\mathfrak g<d<h^\vee$, which contradicts a conjecture of Chen and Ngô and a theorem of Song, Xia and Xu, and it shows directly that a lemma used by Song, Xia and Xu fails for every $d\ge2$.
E.4.1 Setting

Let $k$ be an algebraically closed field of characteristic zero, $G$ a connected reductive group over $k$ with Lie algebra $\mathfrak g$, $\mathfrak h\subset\mathfrak g$ a Cartan subalgebra and $W=N_G(\mathfrak h)/Z_G(\mathfrak h)$.

For $d\ge1$ the commuting scheme $\mathcal C^d_{\mathfrak g}\subset\mathfrak g^d$ is the scheme-theoretic zero fibre of $(x_1,\ldots,x_d)\mapsto([x_i,x_j])_{i<j}$, so $k[\mathcal C^d_{\mathfrak g}]=k[\mathfrak g^d]/I_d$ with $I_d$ generated by the coordinate functions of all $[x_i,x_j]$, and restriction along $\mathfrak h^d\subset\mathcal C^d_{\mathfrak g}$ defines
\Phi:\ k[\mathcal C^d_{\mathfrak g}]^G\longrightarrow k[\mathfrak h^d]^W.\tag{E.12}
For $d=1$ this is the Chevalley restriction isomorphism.

Chen and Ngô conjectured that $\Phi$ is an isomorphism for every reductive $G$ and every $d$, equivalently that $\mathcal C^d_{\mathfrak g}/\!\!/G$ is reduced and normal [32, Conjecture 3.1]; their weaker Conjecture 3.2, the existence of a spectral data morphism, already forces $\Phi$ to be injective [32, Section 3].
The conjecture is a theorem for $GL_n$ [42; 43; 32, Theorem 3.3] and for $Sp_{2n}$ [33, Theorem 4.1], and Song, Xia and Xu state it for $O_n$ and $SO_n$ [34, Theorem 1.2].

For $d=2$ it holds for every connected reductive group by [46, Theorem 1.4.11] and the normality of $\mathcal C^2_{\mathfrak g}$ proved in [47], see also [48] for $\mathfrak g_2$; for the reduced schemes, $\mathfrak h^d/\!\!/W\to(\mathcal C^d_{\mathfrak g})_{\mathrm{red}}/\!\!/G$ is an isomorphism in types A–D and $G_2$ [44], building on [45].
Fix a nondegenerate invariant symmetric form $B$ on $\mathfrak g$ and set
T(x)=\bigl(B(x_i,x_j)\bigr)_{1\le i,j\le d},\qquad \det T\in k[\mathfrak g^d]^G_{2d}.\tag{E.13}

Under $GL_d$ acting on $(x_1,\ldots,x_d)$, $\det T$ transforms by $\det^2$, so it lies in the $SL_d$-invariant part of degree $2d$; when $d>\operatorname{rk}\mathfrak g$, any $d$ vectors of $\mathfrak h$ are linearly dependent and $\det T|_{\mathfrak h^d}=0$.
The question is whether $\det T$ lies in $I_d$.

For three adjoint scalars and the trace form of a representation, $\det T=\tfrac16\varepsilon_{IJK}\varepsilon_{LMN}\operatorname{tr}(\gamma^I\gamma^L)\operatorname{tr}(\gamma^J\gamma^M)\operatorname{tr}(\gamma^K\gamma^N)$.
Definition E.4.

*Let $E$ be a finite-dimensional super vector space. The commuting superscheme $\mathcal C_E$ has coordinate superalgebra $\mathcal O(\mathcal C_E)=\mathrm{Sym}(E\otimes\mathfrak g^*)/J_E$, where $J_E$ is generated by the functions $\theta\mapsto\xi([\theta(e),\theta(e')])$ for $e,e'\in E$, $\xi\in\mathfrak g^*$. Its points over a supercommutative algebra $R$ are the even elements $\theta$ of $\mathrm{Hom}(E,\mathfrak g)\otimes R$ with $[\theta(e),\theta(e')]=0$. The group $GL(E)\times G$ acts, and the Cartan restriction is $\Phi_E:\mathcal O(\mathcal C_E)^G\to\mathcal O(\mathrm{Hom}(E,\mathfrak h))^W$.*
For $E=k^d$ this is the commuting scheme, and for $E=k^{d_B|d_F}$ the super-commuting scheme of [29, Section 2].
The decisive input is the classical chiral ring of $\mathcal N=1$ super-Yang–Mills theory.
Theorem E.5 (Cachazo–Douglas–Seiberg–Witten).

*Let $\mathfrak g$ be simple with dual Coxeter number $h^\vee$, $(e_a)$ a basis of $\mathfrak g$ and $X^a,Y^a$ odd generators. Put $X=\sum_ae_a\otimes X^a$, $Y=\sum_ae_a\otimes Y^a$, and let $A$ be the quotient of $\Lambda(X^a,Y^a)$ by the coordinates of $\{X,X\}=\{X,Y\}=\{Y,Y\}=0$, where $\{X,Y\}=\sum_{a,b}[e_a,e_b]\otimes X^aY^b$. Let $S=\sum_{a,b}B(e_a,e_b)X^aY^b$. Then (i) $A^{\mathfrak g}$ is generated by $S$, (ii) $S^{h^\vee}=0$, and (iii) $S^{h^\vee-1}\ne0$.*

This is the conjecture of [3], proved in part (i) for every simple $\mathfrak g$ in [39], in parts (i)–(iii) for classical $\mathfrak g$ in [3; 40; 41], for $\mathfrak g_2$ in [35], and for $\mathfrak f_4,\mathfrak e_6,\mathfrak e_7,\mathfrak e_8$ in [38].
In the notation of Definition E.4, $A=\mathcal O(\mathcal C_{\Pi k^2})$, where $\Pi k^2$ is purely odd of dimension $0|2$.
E.4.2 The transfer
Lemma E.6.
*Let $\Lambda=\Lambda[u_1,\ldots,u_d,v_1,\ldots,v_d]$ be the exterior algebra on odd generators and $N_{ij}=u_iv_j+u_jv_i\in\Lambda_{\bar0}$. Then*
\det(N_{ij})_{1\le i,j\le d}=(d+1)!\;u_1v_1u_2v_2\cdots u_dv_d.\tag{E.14}
*Proof.* Adjoin odd variables $\theta_i,\bar\theta_i$ and let $\int$ extract the coefficient of $\bar\theta_1\theta_1\cdots\bar\theta_d\theta_d$.

For a matrix $M$ with entries in the commutative ring $\Lambda_{\bar0}$, the top component of $\exp(\sum_{i,j}\bar\theta_iM_{ij}\theta_j)$ is $\frac1{d!}(\sum_{i,j}\bar\theta_iM_{ij}\theta_j)^d=\sum_{\sigma\in S_d}\prod_rM_{r\sigma(r)}\bar\theta_r\theta_{\sigma(r)}=\det M\,\bar\theta_1\theta_1\cdots\bar\theta_d\theta_d$, since reordering the odd $\theta$'s among the even pairs produces $\operatorname{sgn}\sigma$; hence $\det M=\int\exp(\bar\theta M\theta)$.

For $M=N$, with the even elements $\alpha=\sum_i\bar\theta_iu_i$, $\beta=\sum_jv_j\theta_j$, $\gamma=\sum_i\bar\theta_iv_i$, $\varepsilon=\sum_ju_j\theta_j$, one has $\bar\theta_iu_jv_i\theta_j=-\bar\theta_iv_i\,u_j\theta_j$, so $\sum_{i,j}\bar\theta_iN_{ij}\theta_j=\alpha\beta-\gamma\varepsilon$ and, as $\alpha,\beta,\gamma,\varepsilon$ commute, $\det N=\int\sum_{r+s=d}\frac{(-1)^s}{r!\,s!}\alpha^r\gamma^s\beta^r\varepsilon^s$.

Expanding, $\alpha^r\gamma^s=r!\,s!\sum_{I\sqcup J=[d],|I|=r}\prod_{i\in I}\bar\theta_iu_i\prod_{j\in J}\bar\theta_jv_j$ and $\beta^r\varepsilon^s=r!\,s!\sum_{K\sqcup L=[d],|K|=r}\prod_{i\in K}v_i\theta_i\prod_{j\in L}u_j\theta_j$; a product is nonzero exactly when $K=I$ and $L=J$.

Then $\bar\theta_iu_i\,v_i\theta_i=\bar\theta_i\theta_i\,u_iv_i$ and $\bar\theta_jv_j\,u_j\theta_j=-\bar\theta_j\theta_j\,u_jv_j$, so each surviving term equals $(-1)^s\prod_mu_mv_m$ times the top monomial.
Collecting, $\det N=\sum_{r=0}^d\frac{(-1)^s}{r!\,s!}(r!\,s!)^2\binom dr(-1)^s\prod_mu_mv_m=\sum_{r=0}^dd!\prod_mu_mv_m=(d+1)!\prod_mu_mv_m$.
Proposition E.7.

*Let $\mathfrak g$ be simple, $A$ as in Theorem E.5, $\Lambda$ as in Lemma E.6, and $R_d=(A\otimes\Lambda)_{\bar0}$. Put $x_i=Xu_i+Yv_i=\sum_ae_a\otimes(X^au_i+Y^av_i)\in\mathfrak g\otimes R_d$. Then (i) $[x_i,x_j]=0$ for all $i,j$; (ii) $B(x_i,x_j)=-S\,(u_iv_j+u_jv_i)$; (iii) the homomorphism $\varphi:k[\mathcal C^d_{\mathfrak g}]\to R_d$ defined by $(x_1,\ldots,x_d)$ satisfies $\varphi(\det T)=(-1)^d(d+1)!\,S^d\otimes u_1v_1\cdots u_dv_d$.*
*Proof.* (i) Moving the odd $u_i$ or $v_i$ past one odd generator, $[x_i,x_j]=-\sum_{a,b}[e_a,e_b]\otimes(X^aX^bu_iu_j+X^aY^bu_iv_j+Y^aX^bv_iu_j+Y^aY^bv_iv_j)$.

The four coefficients are $\{X,X\}$, $\{X,Y\}$, $\{Y,X\}=\{X,Y\}$ and $\{Y,Y\}$; for instance $XX=\tfrac12\sum_{a,b}[e_a,e_b]X^aX^b$ in $U(\mathfrak g)\otimes A$, so $XX+XX=\sum_{a,b}[e_a,e_b]X^aX^b$. All four vanish in $A$.

(ii) With $B_{ab}=B(e_a,e_b)$, $B(x_i,x_j)=-\sum_{a,b}B_{ab}(X^aX^bu_iu_j+X^aY^bu_iv_j+Y^aX^bv_iu_j+Y^aY^bv_iv_j)$; symmetry of $B_{ab}$ and antisymmetry of $X^aX^b$, $Y^aY^b$ remove the first and last terms, and $\sum B_{ab}Y^aX^b=-S$ with $v_iu_j=-u_jv_i$ gives the claim.
(iii) By (i) the evaluation $k[\mathfrak g^d]\to R_d$ kills $I_d$; by (ii) and Lemma E.6, with $S$ even, $\varphi(\det T)=\det(-S\,N_{ij})=(-S)^d\det N$.
Corollary E.8.
*If $d<h^\vee$, then $\det T\notin I_d$.*
*Proof.* By Theorem E.5(iii), $S^d\ne0$ in $A$ for $d\le h^\vee-1$.
The algebra $A\otimes\Lambda$ is free over $A$ on the monomials in $u,v$, so $S^d\otimes u_1v_1\cdots u_dv_d\ne0$, and Proposition E.7(iii) gives $\varphi(\det T)\ne0$.
Since $\varphi$ factors through $k[\mathcal C^d_{\mathfrak g}]=k[\mathfrak g^d]/I_d$, the class of $\det T$ is nonzero.
E.4.3 The Gram component
Lemma E.9.

*For each $n\ge0$ there is a $G\times S_n$-module $V_n$, independent of $E$, with natural isomorphisms $\mathcal O(\mathcal C_E)_n\cong(E^{\otimes n}\otimes V_n)_{S_n}$, where $S_n$ permutes the tensor factors of $E^{\otimes n}$ with Koszul signs and those of $V_n$.*
*Proof.* The supersymmetric power is $\mathrm{Sym}^n(E\otimes\mathfrak g^*)=(E^{\otimes n}\otimes(\mathfrak g^*)^{\otimes n})_{S_n}$.

Let $c:\mathfrak g^*\to(\mathfrak g^*)^{\otimes2}$ be the transpose of the bracket and $K_2=c(\mathfrak g^*)$, a space of antisymmetric tensors; the generator $\theta\mapsto\xi([\theta(e),\theta(e')])$ of $J_E$ is the class of $e\otimes e'\otimes c(\xi)$.
Hence the degree-$n$ part of $J_E$ is $(E^{\otimes n}\otimes K_n)_{S_n}$ for the $S_n$-submodule $K_n\subset(\mathfrak g^*)^{\otimes n}$ generated by $K_2\otimes(\mathfrak g^*)^{\otimes(n-2)}$.
Coinvariants are exact in characteristic zero, so $\mathcal O(\mathcal C_E)_n=(E^{\otimes n}\otimes V_n)_{S_n}$ with $V_n=(\mathfrak g^*)^{\otimes n}/K_n$.

By super Schur–Weyl duality [49; 50], for a partition $\lambda\vdash n$ with Specht module $\mathrm{Sp}_\lambda$ the super Schur functor $\mathbb S_\lambda(E)=(E^{\otimes n}\otimes\mathrm{Sp}_\lambda)_{S_n}$ is nonzero for $E=k^{m|p}$ if and only if $\lambda_{m+1}\le p$; the nonzero $\mathbb S_\lambda(E)$ are irreducible and pairwise non-isomorphic $GL(E)$-modules, $\mathbb S_\lambda(\Pi k^e)\cong\mathbb S_{\lambda'}(k^e)$ with $\lambda'$ the transpose partition, and $\mathrm{Sym}(E\otimes F)=\bigoplus_\lambda\mathbb S_\lambda(E)\otimes\mathbb S_\lambda(F)$ for $F$ purely even.
Writing $V_n=\bigoplus_{\lambda\vdash n}\mathrm{Sp}_\lambda\otimes M_\lambda$ with $M_\lambda=\mathrm{Hom}_{S_n}(\mathrm{Sp}_\lambda,V_n)$, Lemma E.9 gives

\mathcal O(\mathcal C_E)_n=\bigoplus_{\lambda\vdash n}\mathbb S_\lambda(E)\otimes M_\lambda,\qquad \mathcal O(\mathcal C_E)^G_n=\bigoplus_{\lambda\vdash n}\mathbb S_\lambda(E)\otimes M^G_\lambda.\tag{E.15}
Lemma E.10.

*For each $\lambda\vdash n$ there is a linear map $\phi_\lambda:M^G_\lambda\to\mathbb S_\lambda(\mathfrak h^*)^W$, independent of $E$, with $\Phi_E=\bigoplus_\lambda\mathrm{id}_{\mathbb S_\lambda(E)}\otimes\phi_\lambda$. In particular $\Phi_E$ vanishes on $\mathbb S_\lambda(E)\otimes M^G_\lambda$ when $\lambda$ has more than $\operatorname{rk}\mathfrak g$ parts.*
*Proof.* Restriction $\mathfrak g^*\to\mathfrak h^*$ induces an $S_n$-equivariant map $(\mathfrak g^*)^{\otimes n}\to(\mathfrak h^*)^{\otimes n}$, which kills $K_n$ because $\mathfrak h$ is abelian.

Applying $(E^{\otimes n}\otimes-)_{S_n}$ to the induced map $V_n\to(\mathfrak h^*)^{\otimes n}$ gives the restriction $\mathcal O(\mathcal C_E)_n\to\mathrm{Sym}^n(E\otimes\mathfrak h^*)$, and $\mathrm{Hom}_{S_n}(\mathrm{Sp}_\lambda,(\mathfrak h^*)^{\otimes n})=\mathbb S_\lambda(\mathfrak h^*)$.
Taking $G$-invariants on the source, whose image is $W$-invariant, gives $\phi_\lambda$; finally $\mathbb S_\lambda(\mathfrak h^*)=0$ when $\lambda$ has more than $\dim\mathfrak h$ parts.
Theorem E.11 (Gram component).

*Let $\mathfrak g$ be simple, $G$ connected and $d\ge1$. There is a vector space $L_d$, independent of $E$, such that for every finite-dimensional super vector space $E$ the $\mathbb S_{(2^d)}(E)$-isotypic component of $\mathcal O(\mathcal C_E)^G_{2d}$ is*
\mathcal O(\mathcal C_E)^G_{(2^d)}\cong\mathbb S_{(2^d)}(E)\otimes L_d,\qquad \dim L_d=\begin{cases}1,&d<h^\vee,\\ 0,&d\ge h^\vee,\end{cases}\tag{E.16}

*where $(2^d)=(2,\ldots,2)$ has $d$ parts. For $E=k^d$ this component is the $SL_d$-invariant subspace of degree $2d$ of $k[\mathcal C^d_{\mathfrak g}]^G$, and for $d<h^\vee$ it is spanned by the class of $\det T$.*

*Proof.* By [(E.15)](#eq-E-decomp) and super Schur–Weyl duality, the $\mathbb S_{(2^d)}(E)$-isotypic component of $\mathcal O(\mathcal C_E)^G_{2d}$ is $\mathbb S_{(2^d)}(E)\otimes L_d$ with $L_d=M^G_{(2^d)}$, independent of $E$.

Odd side: for $E=\Pi k^2$, $\mathbb S_\lambda(\Pi k^2)=\mathbb S_{\lambda'}(k^2)$, which contains $SL_2$-invariants exactly for $\lambda'=(c,c)$; in degree $2d$ this selects $\lambda=(2^d)$, and $\mathbb S_{(d,d)}(k^2)=\det^d$ is one-dimensional, so $(A^G_{2d})^{SL_2}\cong L_d$.

By Theorem E.5(i), $A^G$ is generated by $S$, of degree $2$, and $S\mapsto\det(g)S$ under $(X,Y)\mapsto(g_{11}X+g_{12}Y,g_{21}X+g_{22}Y)$ because $B(X,X)=B(Y,Y)=0$ and $B(Y,X)=-B(X,Y)$; so $(A^G_{2d})^{SL_2}=k\,S^d$, of dimension $1$ for $d<h^\vee$ and $0$ for $d\ge h^\vee$ by Theorem E.5(ii),(iii).

Even side: for $E=k^d$, $\mathbb S_\lambda(k^d)$ with $\lambda\vdash2d$ contains $SL_d$-invariants exactly for $\lambda=(2^d)$, where it is $\det^2$; so the $SL_d$-invariant subspace of degree $2d$ is $L_d$, and it contains the class of $\det T$, which is nonzero for $d<h^\vee$ by Corollary E.8 and therefore spans it.
E.4.4 Cartan restriction and nilpotency
Lemma E.12.

*Let $\mathfrak g$ be semisimple and $(x_1,\ldots,x_d)\in\mathcal C^d_{\mathfrak g}(k)$ with Jordan decompositions $x_i=s_i+n_i$. Then $s_1,\ldots,s_d$ lie in one Cartan subalgebra and $f(x_1,\ldots,x_d)=f(s_1,\ldots,s_d)$ for every $f\in k[\mathfrak g^d]^G$.*

*Proof.* Each $\operatorname{ad}s_i$ and $\operatorname{ad}n_i$ is a polynomial in $\operatorname{ad}x_i$, so all $s_i,n_j$ commute pairwise, and the $s_i$ span a toral subalgebra contained in a Cartan subalgebra.

Let $L=Z_G(s_1,\ldots,s_d)^\circ$, with Lie algebra $\mathfrak z_{\mathfrak g}(s_1,\ldots,s_d)$; the commuting nilpotent $n_i$ lie in the nilradical of a Borel subalgebra $\mathfrak b$ of this Lie algebra.
For a cocharacter $\mu$ of a maximal torus of $L$ pairing positively with every root of that nilradical, $\mu(t)\cdot x_i=s_i+\mu(t)\cdot n_i\to s_i$ as $t\to0$, and $f(x)=f(\mu(t)\cdot x)\to f(s)$.
The argument follows [45], [44, Section 6] and [32, Section 3].
Corollary E.13.

*Let $\mathfrak g$ be simple with $\operatorname{rk}\mathfrak g<d<h^\vee$. Then the class of $\det T$ in $k[\mathcal C^d_{\mathfrak g}]^G$ is nonzero and nilpotent, and $\Phi(\det T)=0$. Consequently $\ker\Phi\ne0$, the nilradical of $k[\mathcal C^d_{\mathfrak g}]^G$ is nonzero, and Conjectures 3.1 and 3.2 of [32] fail for $(\mathfrak g,d)$.*
*Proof.* By Corollary E.8, the class of $\det T$ is nonzero.
Since $d>\dim\mathfrak h$, vectors $x_1,\ldots,x_d\in\mathfrak h$ are linearly dependent, so $\Phi(\det T)=0$, equivalently Lemma E.10 with $\lambda=(2^d)$.

At every $k$-point of $\mathcal C^d_{\mathfrak g}$, Lemma E.12 gives $\det T(x)=\det T(s)$ with $s_1,\ldots,s_d$ in a Cartan subalgebra of dimension $\operatorname{rk}\mathfrak g<d$, so $\det T(x)=0$; by the Nullstellensatz $\det T\in\sqrt{I_d}$, and its class is a nonzero nilpotent element.
Conjecture 3.1 of [32] asserts that $\Phi$ is an isomorphism, and Conjecture 3.2 implies that $\Phi$ is injective [32, Section 3].

E.4.6 The orthogonal case of Song, Xia and Xu

For $G=O_n$, and for $G=SO_n$ with $n$ odd, [34, Theorem 1.2] is [34, Theorem 3.4], deduced from [34, Proposition 3.1, Lemmas 3.2, 3.3]; for the orthogonal groups the degree bound [34, Lemma 3.3] is deduced in [34, Section 5.2] from [34, Lemma 5.3], whose proof invokes [34, Lemma 5.2] for the same $d$.
For $SO_{2m}$ the proof of [34, Theorem 4.3] uses [34, Theorem 3.4] for $O_{2m}$; the symplectic case rests on the Pfaffian of Chen and Ngô and is independent of [34, Lemma 5.2].

Let $(t_{ij})$ be the generic skew-symmetric $(2d+3)\times(2d+3)$ matrix, $h_{i_1\cdots i_k}$ the Pfaffian of the matrix obtained by deleting rows and columns $i_1,\ldots,i_k$ (a repeated index leaves a matrix of odd size, so it gives zero), and $\mathsf A$ the $2d\times2d$ matrix of [34, Section 5.2],
[34, Lemma 5.2] asserts that $h_{2d+2}=0$ and $h_{2d+3}\det\mathsf A\ne0$ have a common solution.
Theorem E.16.
*On the hypersurface $h_{2d+2}=0$ the matrix $\mathsf A$ has rank at most $3$. Consequently $\det\mathsf A\in(h_{2d+2})$ for every $d\ge2$, and [34, Lemma 5.2] fails for every $d\ge2$.*

*Proof.* Let $P$ be the skew-symmetric matrix of size $2d+2$ obtained from $(t_{ij})$ by deleting row and column $2d+2$, so $\operatorname{Pf}P=h_{2d+2}$; its rows and columns $1,\ldots,2d+1$ are those of $(t_{ij})$, and its last one is the original $2d+3$.

For $1\le a<b\le2d+2$ put $P^\sharp_{ab}=(-1)^{a+b}\operatorname{Pf}P(\hat a,\hat b)$ and $P^\sharp_{ba}=-P^\sharp_{ab}$; expansion of the Pfaffian along a row gives $PP^\sharp=(\operatorname{Pf}P)\mathbf 1$, and $h_{i,j,2d+2}=\pm P^\sharp_{ij}$, $h_{i,2d+1,2d+2}=\pm P^\sharp_{i,2d+1}$ for $i,j\le2d$.

On $\operatorname{Pf}P=0$ the columns of $P^\sharp$ lie in $\ker P$; if $\operatorname{rk}P=2d$ this kernel has dimension $2$, and if $\operatorname{rk}P\le2d-2$ every principal submatrix of size $2d$ is singular and $P^\sharp=0$.

In both cases the skew matrix $P^\sharp$ has rank at most $2$, hence $P^\sharp=vw^{\mathsf T}-wv^{\mathsf T}$, and squares remove the signs: $h^2_{i,j,2d+2}=(v_iw_j-v_jw_i)^2$ and $h^2_{i,2d+1,2d+2}=\ell_i^2$ with $\ell_i=w_{2d+1}v_i-v_{2d+1}w_i$.
With $f_i=(v_i^2,w_i^2,v_iw_i,1)$, $a=w_{2d+1}^2$, $b=v_{2d+1}^2$ and $c=-2w_{2d+1}v_{2d+1}$, expanding the squares gives $\mathsf A_{ij}=f_iMf_j^{\mathsf T}$ with
\begin{gathered}M=\begin{pmatrix}0&1&0&a\\1&0&0&b\\0&0&-2&c\\a&b&c&0\end{pmatrix},\\ \det M=-2\det\begin{pmatrix}0&1&a\\1&0&b\\a&b&0\end{pmatrix}+c^2=-4ab+c^2=0.\end{gathered}\tag{E.21}
Thus $\operatorname{rk}\mathsf A\le\operatorname{rk}M\le3<2d$, and $\det\mathsf A$ vanishes at every $k$-point of $h_{2d+2}=0$.
The Pfaffian $h_{2d+2}$ is irreducible [51, Lemma B.2.10], so $(h_{2d+2})$ is prime and the Nullstellensatz gives $\det\mathsf A\in(h_{2d+2})$.

The proof uses polynomial identities over $\mathbb Z$ and linear algebra over a field of characteristic different from $2$, so [34, Lemma 5.2] also fails in characteristic $p>2$ for $d\ge2$, and the proofs of [34, Theorems 3.5, 4.4] for the orthogonal groups are incomplete for $d\ge2$.

The step that breaks is the induction in the proof of [34, Lemma 5.2], which asserts that $\det\mathsf A$ has degree at most $4d-4$ in $t_{12}$ with a leading coefficient given by the product of a $2\times2$ determinant and the matrix of the same form for the matrix with rows and columns $1,2$ deleted.

For $j\ge3$ the entries $\mathsf A_{1j}$ and $\mathsf A_{2j}$ contain $h^2_{j,2d+1,2d+2}$, of degree $2$ in $t_{12}$; the leading $t_{12}^2$ parts of rows $1$ and $2$ coincide, so the coefficient of $t_{12}^{4d}$ vanishes, the exact degree is $4d-2$ at $d=2,3$, and at random integer values of the other $t_{ij}$ the coefficient of $t_{12}^{4d-4}$ differs from the asserted product.
The base case $d=1$ is correct: there $\det\mathsf A=-(t_{35}^2+(t_{25}+t_{15})^2)(t_{35}^2+(t_{25}-t_{15})^2)$, and Theorem E.16 holds trivially because $2d=2\le3$.
At random rational points of $h_{2d+2}=0$, $\operatorname{rk}\mathsf A=2$ and $\det\mathsf A\ne0$ for $d=1$, and $\operatorname{rk}\mathsf A=3$, $\det\mathsf A=0$ for $d=2,3,4$.
Corollary E.17.

*Let $n=2m+1\ge7$ with $m+1\le d\le2m-2$, or $n=2m\ge8$ with $m+1\le d\le2m-3$. For $G=O_n$ and $G=SO_n$ the restriction $\Phi:k[\mathcal C^d_{\mathfrak{so}_n}]^G\to k[\mathfrak h^d]^W$ has a nonzero kernel and $k[\mathcal C^d_{\mathfrak{so}_n}]^G$ has a nonzero nilradical. In particular [34, Theorem 1.2(1), Corollary 1.3] fail for $n=7$, $d=4$, and the degree bound [34, Lemma 3.3] and [34, Lemma 5.3], which implies it, are false for $G=O_n$ and for $G=SO_n$ with $n$ odd in the same range.*
*Proof.* These are the pairs $(B_m,d)$ and $(D_m,d)$ of the table above; Corollary E.13 gives the statement for $SO_n$, and $\det T$ is $O_n$-invariant, so the same element works for $O_n$.
Since [34, Proposition 3.1, Lemma 3.2] are independent of [34, Section 5.2] and [34, Theorem 3.4] follows formally from them and [34, Lemma 3.3], that lemma must fail.
E.4.7 Super-commuting schemes and N=4 theory

By Chang and Yin [1], the classical $Q$-cohomology of $\mathcal N=4$ super-Yang–Mills theory with gauge algebra $\mathfrak g$ is the relative Lie algebra cohomology $H^\bullet(\mathfrak g[\mathsf A],\mathfrak g;\mathbb C)$ with $\mathsf A=\mathbb C[z_+,z_-]\otimes\Lambda(\theta_1,\theta_2,\theta_3)$.

By [29, Proposition 4], its part of top degree $p=|n|$ and multidegree $n=(n_{z_+},n_{z_-},n_{\theta_1},n_{\theta_2},n_{\theta_3})$ is $\mathcal O(\mathcal C_{k^{3|2}})^G_n$, the three even coordinates being the $\theta_i$-components and the two odd ones the $z_\pm$-components of the BPS superfield.

In the notation of Appendix [E.1.1](#sec-E-sectors), the multidegree $n$ is the sector weight $(n_{\theta_1},n_{\theta_2},n_{\theta_3};n_{z_+},n_{z_-})$ and the top degree is the number of letters $Y=p$.
Corollary E.18.

*Let $\mathfrak g$ be simple and $1\le d<h^\vee$. For the Borel subalgebra of $\mathfrak{gl}(3|2)$ with the even basis vectors first, $\mathbb S_{(2^d)}(k^{3|2})$ is nonzero with highest weight $\bigl((2^{\min(d,3)},0^{3-\min(d,3)})\,|\,(c,c)\bigr)$, $c=\max(d-3,0)$. Hence $\mathcal O(\mathcal C_{k^{3|2}})^G$ contains $\mathbb S_{(2^d)}(k^{3|2})\otimes L_d\ne0$, of degree $2d$, whose highest-weight vector lies in the sector $(2,0,0;0,0)_2$, $(2,2,0;0,0)_4$ or $(2,2,2;d-3,d-3)_{2d}$ for $d=1$, $d=2$ or $d\ge3$. Its part in the sector $(0,0,0;d,d)_{2d}$ is $k\,S^d$ with $S=B(X,Y)$ for the two odd coordinates. For $d>\operatorname{rk}\mathfrak g$ this component lies in $\ker\Phi_{k^{3|2}}$.*

*Proof.* The hook condition $\lambda_4\le2$ holds for $\lambda=(2^d)$, and for the distinguished Borel subalgebra the highest weight of $\mathbb S_\lambda(k^{3|2})$ is $(\lambda_1,\lambda_2,\lambda_3\,|\,\max(\lambda'_1-3,0),\max(\lambda'_2-3,0))$ [50], which for $\lambda=(2^d)$ is the stated weight.

Write $k^{3|2}=k^3\oplus\Pi k^2$; in Lemma E.9 the part of $E^{\otimes n}$ of degree zero in $k^3$ is $(\Pi k^2)^{\otimes n}$, so the part of $\mathcal O(\mathcal C_{k^{3|2}})$ of degree zero in the even coordinates is $\mathcal O(\mathcal C_{\Pi k^2})=A$, and the corresponding part of $\mathbb S_{(2^d)}(k^{3|2})$ is $\mathbb S_{(2^d)}(\Pi k^2)=\det^d$.
By the odd side of the proof of Theorem E.11, this part of the component is $(A^G_{2d})^{SL_2}=k\,S^d$; the rest follows from Theorem E.11 and Lemma E.10.
Corollary E.19.

*If $\Phi_{k^d}$ is an isomorphism for every $d\ge1$, then $\Phi_E$ is an isomorphism for every finite-dimensional super vector space $E$. In particular, for $\mathfrak g=\mathfrak{sp}_{2N}$ the map $\Phi_{k^{3|2}}$ is an isomorphism, and every nonzero element of $\mathcal O(\mathcal C_{k^{3|2}})^G$ has nonzero Cartan restriction.*

*Proof.* By Lemma E.10, $\Phi_{k^d}=\bigoplus_\lambda\mathrm{id}\otimes\phi_\lambda$ with $\mathbb S_\lambda(k^d)\ne0$ for every $\lambda$ with at most $d$ parts, so all $\phi_\lambda$ are isomorphisms, and $\Phi_E=\bigoplus_\lambda\mathrm{id}\otimes\phi_\lambda$ is an isomorphism.
For $\mathfrak{sp}_{2N}$ the hypothesis is [33, Theorem 4.1].
For $\mathfrak g_2$, $d=3$ gives the non-Cartan class of $\det T$ in the purely scalar sector $(2,2,2;0,0)_6$; Appendix [E.5](#sec-E-G2) shows that it survives at every perturbative order.

For $\mathfrak{so}_7$, $d=4$ gives a non-Cartan class in $(2,2,2;1,1)_8$, at level $9$; by [24, Section 3, Table 1], $\mathcal O(\mathcal C_{k^{3|2}})^{SO_7}$ is $85$-dimensional there ($84$ for $\mathfrak{sp}_6$), and super-abelianization, which is $\Phi_{k^{3|2}}$, has a one-dimensional kernel on it, so Corollary E.18 spans this kernel and contains the non-Cartan class of [29, Theorem 1], the target of the one-loop lift of $O_f$ in Appendix [E.3](#sec-E-SOSp).

For the S-dual pair $(\mathfrak{so}_{2N+1},\mathfrak{sp}_{2N})$, with dual Coxeter numbers $2N-1$ and $N+1$, Corollary E.18 gives non-Cartan classes for $\mathfrak{so}_{2N+1}$ in the sectors $(2,2,2;d-3,d-3)_{2d}$ for $N+1\le d\le2N-2$, and by Corollary E.19 the Cartan restriction is injective for $\mathfrak{sp}_{2N}$; for $N=4$ these are $(2,2,2;2,2)_{10}$, with $E=12$, and $(2,2,2;3,3)_{12}$, with $E=15$, both with $R_I=E/3$ and $J_L=J_R=0$.

The odd coordinates are the gaugino components $\lambda_\pm$ of [28, Section 2], and $S$ is a nonzero multiple of $\operatorname{Tr}(\lambda_+\lambda_-)$; for $\operatorname{rk}\mathfrak g<d<h^\vee$ the vector $S^d$ is the non-Coulomb monotone class $[S^d]$ of Kibe, van Leuven and Mathieson [28], and Corollary E.18 places it in one irreducible $\mathfrak{gl}(3|2)$-module with the class in $(2,2,2;d-3,d-3)_{2d}$, in agreement with their finding that $S^4$ of $\mathfrak{so}_7$ is a superconformal descendant of the class in $(2,2,2;1,1)_8$ [28, Section 5].

E.5.1 Realization
The algebra $\mathfrak g_2$ is realized in $\mathfrak{gl}(7)$ as the matrices preserving the symmetric form $\eta_{i\bar\imath}=1$, $\bar\imath=8-i$, and the three-form
\begin{gathered}\phi=e^{123}+2\,e^{567}+e^{147}+e^{246}+e^{345},\\ \sum_d\bigl(A_{da}\phi_{dbc}+A_{db}\phi_{adc}+A_{dc}\phi_{abd}\bigr)=0,\end{gathered}\tag{E.22}
which gives $\dim\mathfrak g_2=14$.

Its Cartan subalgebra is $\{\operatorname{diag}(a_1,a_2,-a_1-a_2,0,a_1+a_2,-a_2,-a_1)\}$, with short roots $\pm(1,0),\pm(0,1),\pm(1,1)$ and long roots $\pm(1,-1),\pm(2,1),\pm(1,2)$ in the coordinates $(a_1,a_2)$.

The realization reproduces $\dim\mathrm{Sym}^k(\mathfrak g_2)^{G_2}=1,1,2,2,2,3,3$ for $k=2,4,\ldots,14$, in agreement with the Casimir degrees $2$ and $6$, $\dim\Lambda^k(\mathfrak g_2)^{G_2}=1$ for $k=0,3,11,14$, and $\dim\mathrm{Hom}_{G_2}(\mathfrak g_2^{\otimes4},\mathbb C)=5$.

The Casimir tensor involves $\phi$, so $Q_1$, $Q_2$ and $Q_3$ are evaluated as explicit sums over the generators; $Q_0Q_1+Q_1Q_0=0$ was checked on $(3,3,3;0,0)_5$, $(4,3,3;0,0)_6$ and $(3,3,2;1,0)_5$, with $275$, $5254$ and $7646$ nonzero entries, and $Q_0Q_2+Q_1^2+Q_2Q_0=0$ on $(4,4,4;0,0)_6$ and $(4,4,3;1,0)_6$, with $32{,}186$ and $2{,}077{,}705$ entries, all without violation.
Products of traces of letter words in the seven-dimensional representation span the exact dimension in every sector computed.

E.6 Two-loop lifts in the Leigh–Strassler deformation
E.6.1 The theory and its sectors
In the Leigh–Strassler deformation [36] of $SU(3)$ theory, with the superpotential of Section [1](#sec-introduction), the cubic interaction is

\begin{gathered}\frac{1+q}4\cdot\frac i{3!}\bigl(\varepsilon_{IJK}C_{ABC}-iS_{IJK}d_{ABC}\bigr)(\gamma^I)^A(\gamma^J)^B(\gamma^K)^C,\\ S_{IJK}=\rho\,|\varepsilon_{IJK}|+h_e\,\delta_{IJK},\qquad \rho=\frac{1-q}{1+q},\qquad h_e=\frac{2h}{1+q},\end{gathered}\tag{E.23}

where $d_{ABC}=2\operatorname{tr}(t_A\{t_B,t_C\})$ and $\delta_{IJK}=1$ for $I=J=K$ and zero otherwise; with $\operatorname{tr}(t_At_B)=\tfrac12\delta_{AB}$, $\operatorname{tr}(t_At_Bt_C)=\tfrac14(d_{ABC}+iC_{ABC})$.

E.6.4 Independence of the two-loop scheme
Nilpotence fixes $Q_2$ only up to $Q_2\mapsto Q_2+\delta$ with $[Q_0,\delta]=0$, modulo $[Q_0,X]$, which changes no $d_r$.
Such a $\delta$ changes the representative of $d_2$ by $\delta\mathcal O_0$ and leaves $E_2$ of the target unchanged.
Proposition E.21.

*Let $\delta$ carry the quantum numbers of $Q_2$, commute with the gauge symmetry, with $SU(2)_R$ and with the clock and shift symmetries, and act on at most three letters. Then $\delta\mathcal O_0=0$ for every source cocycle of the hits at $E+J_L=7,8,\tfrac{17}2$, so $d_2$ there is determined by $Q_0$, $Q_1$ and nilpotence.*
*Proof.* By Proposition E.1 with $n=2$, $\delta$ lowers $\Theta$ by $6$, so it acts on a subword of at most three letters with $\Theta\ge6$.

The sources $(7,0;0,0)_5$ and $(8,0;0,0)_6$ contain no $\mathsf c$, and their words have $\Theta=7,8$ with $5,6$ letters among $\gamma$ ($\Theta=1$), $\beta$ ($2$) and $\mathsf b$ ($3$); they are $\gamma^4\mathsf b$, $\gamma^3\beta^2$ and $\gamma^5\mathsf b$, $\gamma^4\beta^2$, whose three-letter subwords have $\Theta\le5$.
Hence $\delta$ vanishes on the entire source space; there also $Q_2\mathcal O_0=0$.

For $(7,0;1,0)_5$ the subwords reached by $\delta$ are $\partial\mathsf c\,\gamma\,(\gamma^I\beta_I\mathsf b)$ and $\partial\mathsf c\,\gamma\,(\beta_1\beta_2\beta_3)$, and $SU(2)_R$ forces both output letters of $\delta$ to be $\mathsf c$ with two derivatives, so $\delta\mathcal O_0$ lies in one target skeleton of dimension $8$.
There $Q_0$ is injective into the next sector [p], while $Q_0(\delta\mathcal O_0)=-\delta(Q_0\mathcal O_0)=0$; hence $\delta\mathcal O_0=0$.

The admissible $\delta$ that can act on these sources form at most a $25$-parameter family: $(\gamma^I\beta_I\mathsf b)\to\mathsf c\mathsf c$ with colour structures in $\mathrm{Hom}_G(\mathbf 8^{\otimes3},\Lambda^2\mathbf 8)$, of dimension $16$, $(\beta_1\beta_2\beta_3)\to\mathsf c\mathsf c$ with the cyclic part of that space, of dimension $6$, and $(\beta_I\beta_I\beta_I)\to\mathsf c\mathsf c$ for $h\ne0$, of dimension $3$.

Without the $SU(2)_R$ condition the kernel of $Q_0$ on the coarser support has dimension $3$ and reaches one direction of the target $E_2$, which is not along the image of $d_2$, so such a $\delta$ could only raise the rank from $1$ to $2$.

The one- and two-loop kernels used here agree with the explicit operations of Gui, Wang and Williams [14, Section 4.5]: with input edges $1o,2o,3o$ and outputs $\lambda_1,\lambda_3$ at $\lambda_2=0$, their two-loop constant term is $-\tfrac1{24}(\lambda_1\wedge\lambda_3)^2$ against the kernel $\tfrac1{24}(\lambda_P\wedge\lambda_Q)^2$ of $Q_2$, in all twenty derivative patterns with total input order at most three, while the one-loop kernels agree with sign $+1$; the relative sign is a normalization convention fixed here by nilpotence.

E.7 N=2 quiver, SQCD and mass deformations
The question is whether a two-loop lift appears in theories with genuinely $\mathcal N=2$ matter.
E.7.1 The quiver and SQCD

The $\mathbb Z_2$ orbifold quiver with gauge group $SU(N)\times SU(N)$ and couplings $g_1,g_2$ is obtained from the superfield of $SU(2N)$ by keeping $\mathsf c,\mathsf b,\gamma^3,\beta_3$ in the block-diagonal part and $\gamma^{1,2},\beta_{1,2}$ in the off-diagonal part: conjugation by $\operatorname{diag}(\mathbf 1_N,-\mathbf 1_N)$ maps $C(\theta_1,\theta_2,\theta_3)$ to $C(-\theta_1,-\theta_2,\theta_3)$.
Its sectors are graded as in Appendix [E.1.1](#sec-E-sectors), with highest weights of $GL(2)_{12}\times GL(1)_3\times SL(2)$.
Proposition E.23.
*For $\kappa=g_2/g_1\ne0$ the pages of the quiver are isomorphic to those at $\kappa=1$: $E_r(\kappa)\cong E_r(1)$ for every $r$.*
*Proof.* In every term of $Q_n$, including $n=0$, the power of $\kappa^2$ equals the number of letters $\mathsf b$ and $\beta_3$ of the second node consumed minus the number produced.
Hence $Q_n(\kappa)=\phi_\kappa^{-1}Q_n(1)\phi_\kappa$ for all $n$, where $\phi_\kappa$ multiplies each such letter by $\kappa^2$, and the transferred differentials are conjugate.
The $\kappa\to0$ limit decouples the vector multiplet of the second node and gives $\mathcal N=2$ SQCD with $N_f=2N$, whose flavour singlets are computed with the Haar measure of the second node.
